metadata.scope: e_jingyang (308 baronies across k_fujian, k_huainan, k_hunan, k_jiangdong, k_jiangxi, k_liangzhe, k_shannan)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/vanilla English display name of the audited settlement or holding.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation (negative values = BCE; null if no pre-modern attestation was identified).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of the earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.is_historical_867: Boolean: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= 867 CE for the audited barony name.
schema_notes.named_after_post_867_person: Boolean: true if the title name incorporates a person, saint, or dynasty post-dating 867 CE.
schema_notes.eponym_details: Explanatory text for any eponymous origin (both pre-867 and post-867 eponyms); null if not eponymous or unrecorded.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and English translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Object indicating whether a distinct older name strictly attested <= 867 CE exists for the same site or immediate predecessor.
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (typically Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_jianan.first_mention_attestation: 196 CE (Eastern Han Jian'an 1st year: Sun Ce established Jian'an County, named after Emperor Xian's Jian'an era).
b_jianan.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Eastern Han Jian'an reign era (196–220 CE) when Sun Ce petitioned to establish the county in 196 CE.

b_pucheng.first_mention_attestation: 742 CE (Tang Tianbao 1st year: Tangxing County renamed Pucheng County; originally Hanxing in 196 CE, Wuxing in 260 CE, Tangxing in 621 CE).
b_pucheng.etymology_analysis: Compound of pu (riverbank/estuary) + cheng (walled city), adopted in 742 CE in reference to the Nanpu Stream and earlier Minyue fortifications (Linpucheng).

b_chongan.first_mention_attestation: 951 CE (Southern Tang Baoda 9th year: Wenling Town renamed Chong'an Chang; elevated to Chong'an County in 994 CE).
b_chongan.etymology_analysis: Auspicious administrative compound meaning 'lofty peace' (also associated with nearby Chongling/Chongxi), coined in 951 CE and elevated to a county in 994 CE; renamed Wuyishan in 1989.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Nanping local gazetteers (Tang Zhenguan era, c. 630 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Settled as Xinfeng Township at Chanxikou in northern Jianyang County around 630 CE; renamed Wenling Town in 941 CE and Chong'an Chang in 951 CE.

b_jianyang.first_mention_attestation: 376 CE (Eastern Jin Taiyuan era, 376–396 CE: Jianping County renamed Jianyang County; originally established as Jianping County in 205 CE).
b_jianyang.etymology_analysis: Directional/topographic compound combining Jian (from Jian'an/Jianxi) with yang (sunny/north bank), adopting the name Jianyang during the Eastern Jin Taiyuan era.

b_jianpu.first_mention_attestation: 948 CE (Southern Tang Baoda 6th year: Longjin County renamed Jianpu County as the seat of Jianzhou; renamed Nanping County in 1302 CE).
b_jianpu.etymology_analysis: Compound of jian (sword, referencing Jianzhou and the legendary twin swords at Yanpingjin) + pu (riverbank/estuary), introduced by Southern Tang in 948 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Jin / Fujian local gazetteers
older_name_by_867.notes: Established as Nanping County in 196 CE, renamed Yanping County in 379 CE, abolished in 465–471 CE, and later revived as Yanping Town before becoming Longjin (943 CE) and Jianpu (948 CE).

b_shunchang.first_mention_attestation: 933 CE (Later Tang Changxing 4th year / Min Longqi 1st year: Yongshun Chang elevated to Shunchang County).
b_shunchang.etymology_analysis: Auspicious administrative name meaning 'compliant and prosperous' (Yanping Prefecture Gazetteer: 'named for its early submission'), coined when Yongshun Chang became a county in 933 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Shunchang County history / Yanping Prefecture Gazetteer
older_name_by_867.notes: Established in 629 CE (Tang Zhenguan 3rd year) as Jiangshui Chang from two southeastern townships of Jiangle County; renamed Jiangshui Town in 893 CE and Yongshun Chang thereafter.

b_youxi.first_mention_attestation: 741 CE (Tang Kaiyuan 29th year: Youxi County established under Fuzhou, named after the Youxi Stream).
b_youxi.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Youxi (You Stream, also called Shenxi) flowing through the county.

b_sha.first_mention_attestation: 621 CE (Tang Wude 4th year: Shacun County restored and renamed Sha County; originally established as Shacun County in Eastern Jin Yixi era, 405–418 CE).
b_sha.etymology_analysis: Named after the sandy riverbank terrain (Shayuandi) south of the county seat, shortened from Shacun ('Sand Village') to Sha County in 621 CE.

b_jiangle.first_mention_attestation: 260 CE (Eastern Wu Yong'an 3rd year: Jiangle County established under Jian'an Commandery).
b_jiangle.etymology_analysis: Established in 260 CE; traditionally explained as 'General's Joy' from Han/Minyue-era legends of imperial generals feasting on the Jinxi River.

b_yongan.first_mention_attestation: 1452 CE (Ming Jingtai 3rd year: Yong'an County carved out of Sha County and Youxi County following local pacification).
b_yongan.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Ming-era administrative compound meaning 'eternal peace', coined in 1452 CE after suppressing the Deng Maoqi rebellion.

b_shaowu.first_mention_attestation: 291 CE (Western Jin Yuankang 1st year: Zhaowu County renamed Shaowu County to avoid naming taboo on Sima Zhao; originally Zhaowu County in 260 CE).
b_shaowu.etymology_analysis: Originally Zhaowu (260 CE), altered to Shaowu in 291 CE under Western Jin to avoid the personal name of Sima Zhao.

b_guangze.first_mention_attestation: 979 CE (Northern Song Taiping Xingguo 4th year: Caiyan Town elevated to Guangze County).
b_guangze.etymology_analysis: Named in 979 CE after Guangze Township, evoking scenic mountain light and water luster.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Guangze County history / Taiping Huanyu Ji
older_name_by_867.notes: Tang Wude 7th year (624 CE) established Yangning Town under Shaowu County, administering Guangze and Luanfeng townships; renamed Caiyan Town in 958 CE.

b_jianning.first_mention_attestation: 958 CE (Southern Tang Zhongxing 1st year: Yong'an Chang elevated to Jianning County, combining Jianzhou and Yining Army).
b_jianning.etymology_analysis: Portmanteau of Jianzhou (建州) and Yining Army (义宁军), coined in 958 CE when Southern Tang elevated Yong'an Chang to a county.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Jianning County gazetteer / Tang administrative records
older_name_by_867.notes: Established as Sui'an County in 260 CE (later Suicheng County); in 759 CE (Tang Qianyuan 2nd year) split into Guihua and Huanglian Town, later Yong'an Town/Chang.

b_changting.first_mention_attestation: 736 CE (Tang Kaiyuan 24th year: Tingzhou and its seat Changting County established, named after Changting Creek).
b_changting.etymology_analysis: Descriptive compound meaning 'long sandbar', derived from Changting Creek (Yuanhe Junxian Zhi: 'named after Changting Creek').

b_wuping.first_mention_attestation: 736 CE (Tang Kaiyuan 24th year: Wuping Town established under Jian'an Commandery/Tingzhou; merged into Wuping Chang in 946 CE and elevated to Wuping County in 994 CE).
b_wuping.etymology_analysis: Administrative/auspicious compound meaning 'martial pacification', attested as Wuping Town in 736 CE before becoming a county in 994 CE.

b_shanghang.first_mention_attestation: 769 CE (Tang Dali 4th year: Shanghang Chang established at Hulei Xiabao, carved from Longyan; elevated to Shanghang County in 994 CE).
b_shanghang.etymology_analysis: Directional compound meaning 'upper ferry/boat crossing' on the Ting River, attested as Shanghang Chang from 769 CE.

b_ninghua.first_mention_attestation: 742 CE (Tang Tianbao 1st year: Huanglian County renamed Ninghua County; originally Huanglian Town 667 CE, Huanglian County 725 CE).
b_ninghua.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Tang administrative compound meaning 'pacify and civilize', replacing Huanglian County in 742 CE.

b_jinjiang.first_mention_attestation: 718 CE (Tang Kaiyuan 6th year, or 720 CE per some sources: Jinjiang County carved from Nan'an County, named after the Jin River).
b_jinjiang.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Jin River (Jinjiang), which itself was named for Jin-dynasty northern aristocrats who migrated south along its banks.

b_dehua.first_mention_attestation: 933 CE (Min Longqi 1st year / Later Tang Changxing 4th year: Guide Chang of Yongtai County elevated to Dehua County).
b_dehua.etymology_analysis: Confucian administrative compound meaning 'transformation through virtue', coined in 933 CE from the earlier Guide Chang ('Return to Virtue Market').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Quanzhou Prefecture Gazetteer (Tang Zhenyuan era, 785–805 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Carved from Guiyi Township of Yongtai County during the Tang Zhenyuan era (785–805 CE) as Guide Chang.

b_qingxi_1.first_mention_attestation: 955 CE (Southern Tang Baoda 13th year / Later Zhou Xiande 2nd year: Xiaoxi Chang elevated to Qingxi County; renamed Anxi in 1121 CE).
b_qingxi_1.etymology_analysis: Descriptive compound meaning 'clear stream', named in 955 CE after the limpid waters of the local stream (renamed Anxi in 1121 CE).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Anxi County history / Chinese Wikipedia
older_name_by_867.notes: Established in 864 CE (Tang Xiantong 5th year) as Xiaoxi Chang from two northwestern townships of Nan'an County.

b_huichuan_2.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in Quanzhou, Fujian; historical Huichuan is located in Gansu (Weiyuan) or Sichuan (Huili, Ming-era Huichuan Guard).
b_huichuan_2.etymology_analysis: Generic descriptive compound meaning 'converging streams'; no historical settlement named Huichuan is attested in Quanzhou, Fujian.

b_putian.first_mention_attestation: 568 CE (Southern Chen Guangda 2nd year: Putian County first established; re-established in 589 CE and 622 CE).
b_putian.etymology_analysis: Descriptive compound meaning 'sedge/rush fields', referring to reclaimed coastal marshland cultivated into fields.

b_xianyou.first_mention_attestation: 742 CE (Tang Tianbao 1st year: Qingyuan County renamed Xianyou County; originally Qingyuan County 699 CE).
b_xianyou.etymology_analysis: Named in 742 CE after Xianyou Mountain ('Immortals' Roaming'), referencing the Han-era legend of the Nine He Brothers ascending as immortals at Jiuli Lake.

b_xinghua.first_mention_attestation: 979 CE (Northern Song Taiping Xingguo 4th year: Xinghua County established from parts of Putian and Xianyou, serving as seat of Taiping/Xinghua Commandery until 983 CE).
b_xinghua.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Song administrative compound meaning 'rising prosperity and civilization', coined in 979 CE to pacify the Youyangdong region.

b_longxi_1.first_mention_attestation: 507 CE (Southern Liang Tianjian 6th year, or Datong 6th year 540 CE per some sources: Longxi County carved from Jin'an/Nan'an).
b_longxi_1.etymology_analysis: Descriptive compound meaning 'Dragon Stream', referring to the Jiulong River basin.

b_zhangpu.first_mention_attestation: 686 CE (Tang Chuigong 2nd year: Zhangpu County established alongside Zhangzhou).
b_zhangpu.etymology_analysis: Hydronymic -pu compound meaning 'bank/estuary of the Zhang River', established in 686 CE.

b_longyan.first_mention_attestation: 742 CE (Tang Tianbao 1st year: Xinluo County renamed Longyan County; originally established as Xinluo County in 736 CE).
b_longyan.etymology_analysis: Descriptive compound meaning 'Dragon Crag', named after the nearby Longyan Cave/Crag when Xinluo County was renamed in 742 CE.

b_changtai.first_mention_attestation: 955 CE (Southern Tang Baoda 13th year, or 943 CE per some sources: Wu'an Chang elevated to Changtai County).
b_changtai.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Southern Tang compound meaning 'long-lasting peace and prosperity' (长久安泰), coined upon county establishment in 955 CE.

b_changxi.first_mention_attestation: 623 CE (Tang Wude 6th year: Changxi County established on former Wenma County territory, originally Wenma County in 282 CE).
b_changxi.etymology_analysis: Descriptive compound meaning 'Long Stream', established in 623 CE on the site of Western Jin Wenma County.

b_ningde.first_mention_attestation: 933 CE (Later Tang Changxing 4th year / Min Longqi 1st year: Gande Chang elevated to Ningde County).
b_ningde.etymology_analysis: Portmanteau of Ningchuan Township (宁川乡) and Gande Chang (感德场), coined when the Min kingdom elevated Gande Chang to a county in 933 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ningde County history / Chinese Wikipedia
older_name_by_867.notes: Established during the Tang Kaicheng era (836–840 CE) as Gande Chang from Ningchuan of Changxi County and northeastern Gutian County.

b_fuan.first_mention_attestation: 1245 CE (Southern Song Chunyou 5th year: Fu'an County carved from northwestern Changxi County).
b_fuan.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Southern Song administrative compound meaning 'blessed peace' (also echoing Fuzhou), coined in 1245 CE.

b_min.first_mention_attestation: 592 CE (Sui Kaihuang 12th year: Yuanfeng County renamed Min County; the ethnonym/choronym Min is attested from Zhou/Qin times).
b_min.etymology_analysis: Derived from the ancient Min ethnonym and region name (Seven Min / Minyue), adopted as the county name Min County in 592 CE.

b_yongtai.first_mention_attestation: 766 CE (Tang Yongtai 2nd year: Yongtai County carved from Houguan and Youxi counties, named after the Yongtai reign era).
b_yongtai.etymology_analysis: Named directly after Emperor Daizong's Yongtai reign era (765–766 CE) when the county was established in 766 CE.

b_lianjiang.first_mention_attestation: 623 CE (Tang Wude 6th year: Wenma County restored and renamed Lianjiang County).
b_lianjiang.etymology_analysis: Descriptive compound meaning 'Connected Rivers', referencing the Aojiang/Minjiang estuary network when Wenma was renamed in 623 CE.

b_fuqing.first_mention_attestation: 933 CE (Later Tang Changxing 4th year / Min Longqi 1st year: Futang County renamed Fuqing County).
b_fuqing.etymology_analysis: Portmanteau from Yongfu (永福) and Qingyuanli (清源里), coined in 933 CE when Futang County was renamed Fuqing County.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Fuqing City history / Chinese Wikipedia
older_name_by_867.notes: Established as Wan'an County in 699 CE (Tang Shengli 2nd year); renamed Futang County in 742 CE (Tianbao 1st year).

b_gutian.first_mention_attestation: 741 CE (Tang Kaiyuan 29th year: Gutian County established under Fuzhou from western Houguan).
b_gutian.etymology_analysis: Descriptive compound meaning 'old fields', referring to cleared agricultural land at the confluence of the Shuangxi streams.

b_shanyang_2.first_mention_attestation: 411 CE (Eastern Jin Yixi 7th year: Shanyang Commandery established, followed by Shanyang County in 413 CE).
b_shanyang_2.etymology_analysis: Directional -yang compound ('south of the hill'), established as Shanyang Commandery/County in 411–413 CE (immigrated/named after Shanyang in the north).

b_yancheng.first_mention_attestation: 411 CE (Eastern Jin Yixi 7th year: Yandu County renamed Yancheng County due to surrounding salt fields; originally Yandu County in 119 BCE).
b_yancheng.etymology_analysis: Compound of yan (salt) + cheng (walled city), renamed from Yandu in 411 CE because the town was surrounded by coastal saltworks.

b_baoying.first_mention_attestation: 762 CE (Tang Baoying 1st year: Anyi County renamed Baoying County after eight auspicious treasures were presented to Emperor Suzong, who also adopted the Baoying era name).
b_baoying.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Tang Baoying reign era (762 CE), replacing the earlier name Anyi County.

b_xuyi.first_mention_attestation: 221 BCE (Qin dynasty: Xuyi County established under Donghai Commandery, initially written 盱台).
b_xuyi.etymology_analysis: Explained in Shuowen Jiezi as 'widening the eyes to gaze afar', referring to the hilltop seat overlooking the Huai River plain.

b_qingliu.first_mention_attestation: 598 CE (Sui Kaihuang 18th year: Xinchang County renamed Qingliu County as the seat of Chuzhou).
b_qingliu.etymology_analysis: Descriptive compound meaning 'clear flowing current', referencing the Qingliu River in Chuzhou when Xinchang County was renamed in 598 CE.

b_quanjiao.first_mention_attestation: c. 196 BCE (Early Western Han: Quanjiao County established on the site of ancient Chu Jiao territory; attested in Book of Han Geography Treatise).
b_quanjiao.etymology_analysis: Combines Quan (traditionally from the Quan clan or 'complete') with Jiao (from ancient Jiao state / Jiaoling Mountain, where jiao denotes a mountain peak).

b_yongyang.first_mention_attestation: 709 CE (Tang Jinglong 3rd year: Yongyang County carved from Qingliu County; renamed Lai'an County in 958 CE under Southern Tang).
b_yongyang.etymology_analysis: Directional -yang compound named after Mount Yongyang north of the county seat (renamed Lai'an in 958 CE).

b_hailing.first_mention_attestation: 117 BCE (Western Han Yuanshou 6th year: Hailing County established under Linhuai Commandery).
b_hailing.etymology_analysis: Descriptive topographic compound meaning 'sea hill/mound', named for its elevated terrain beside the ancient coastline.

b_rugao.first_mention_attestation: Established as Rugao County (如皋县) in 411 CE (Eastern Jin, Yixi 7), split from Hailing County and named after a coastal village; attested in Jin Shu and Song Shu.
b_rugao.etymology_analysis: Named after a coastal village (如皋村) on elevated marshland along the northern Yangtze estuary; merged into Ninghai in Sui and restored in 952 CE.

b_jinghai.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 937 CE (Yang Wu, Tianzuo 3) as Dongzhou Jinghai Duzhen (东洲静海都镇) in a Langshan cliff inscription by Yao Cun; elevated to Tongzhou (Jinghai Jun) in 958 CE under Later Zhou.
b_jinghai.etymology_analysis: Garrison and coastal town name meaning 'Pacified/Tranquil Sea', established on newly consolidated Yangtze estuary sandbanks in the Five Dynasties period (10th century CE).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Han Shu (Book of Han): Hailing County established in 117 BCE (Western Han Yuanshou 6), administering the broader northern Yangtze delta.
older_name_by_867.notes: Prior to the 10th-century emergence of Jinghai, the Nantong sandbars fell within Hailing County (海陵县, est. 117 BCE) and the Tang-era Dongzhou (东洲) sandbank.

b_jiangdu.first_mention_attestation: Established as Jiangdu County (江都县) and seat of the Kingdom of Jiangdu in 153 BCE (Western Han, Jingdi 4); attested in Han Shu.
b_jiangdu.etymology_analysis: Means 'Metropolis on the Yangtze River', reflecting its role as the Han-era princely capital of Jiangdu and later the southern capital of Sui Emperor Yang.

b_tianchang.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Tianchang County (天长县) in 748 CE (Tang, Tianbao 7) when Emperor Xuanzong renamed his birthday festival from Qianqiu Jie to Tianchang Jie; originally split from Jiangdu and Liuhe as Qianqiu County in 742 CE.
b_tianchang.etymology_analysis: Imperially bestowed name from 'Tianchang Jie' (天长节, 'Heaven-Enduring Festival'), commemorating Tang Emperor Xuanzong's birthday in 748 CE.

b_gaoyou.first_mention_attestation: In 223 BCE (Qin Wang Zheng 24), Qin built a high terrace and relay post station (Gaoyou Ting, 高邮亭); formally established as Gaoyou County in 118 BCE (Western Han, Yuanshou 5).
b_gaoyou.etymology_analysis: Means 'High Relay Post', named after the elevated Qin-dynasty postal station (高邮亭) constructed to transmit dispatches across the Huai-Yangtze marshes.

b_liuhe.first_mention_attestation: Established as Liuhe County (六合县) in 584 CE (Sui, Kaihuang 4) by merging Yushi, Tangyi, and Fangshan counties; attested in Sui Shu.
b_liuhe.etymology_analysis: Named after the Sui-era Liuhe Commandery (六合郡) or the cosmological 'six directions' (heaven, earth, and four cardinal points), formed on the ancient Qin county of Tangyi (221 BCE).

b_dingcheng.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Dingcheng County (定城县) in 570 CE (Northern Qi, Wuping 1), serving as seat of Yiyang Commandery and later Guangzhou from 712 CE; attested in Sui Shu and Xin Tang Shu.
b_dingcheng.etymology_analysis: Means 'Pacified Walled City', established during the Northern and Southern Dynasties on the site of earlier Yiyang County (206 BCE) and the Zhou-era State of Huang.

b_gushi.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Gushi County (固始县) in 26 CE (Eastern Han, Jianwu 2) when Emperor Guangwu enfeoffed Li Tong as Marquis of Gushi; previously Qin/Western Han Qin County (寝县).
b_gushi.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Han-dynasty name meaning 'Firm Beginning', bestowed by Emperor Guangwu upon Li Tong's marquisate in 26 CE.

b_yincheng_1.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yincheng County (殷城县) in 584 CE (Sui, Kaihuang 4) from Qiao-Baoxin County; attested in Sui Shu and Xin Tang Shu (later renamed Shangcheng in 960 CE to avoid Song Taizu's father's taboo name).
b_yincheng_1.etymology_analysis: Named 'Yin City' (殷城) in Sui Kaihuang 4 (584 CE); in 960 CE (Song Jianlong 1) renamed Shangcheng (商城) to observe the naming taboo of Zhao Hongyin.

b_guangshan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Guangshan County (光山县) in 598 CE (Sui, Kaihuang 18), split from Le'an County; attested in Sui Shu and Xin Tang Shu.
b_guangshan.etymology_analysis: Named directly after Mount Guang (光山) in southeastern Henan, after which Guang Prefecture (光州) was also named.

b_zhongli.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Spring and Autumn period as the State of Zhongli (钟离国, c. 538 BCE in Zuo Zhuan and excavated royal tombs); established as Zhongli County by Qin in 223 BCE.
b_zhongli.etymology_analysis: Originally written 童丽 in bronze inscriptions, Zhongli (钟离) is a sinicized transcription of a Huaiyi (Dongyi) tribal/state name from the Spring and Autumn period.

b_dingyuan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Dingyuan County and Dingyuan Commandery (定远郡/县) in 504 CE (Southern Liang, Tianjian 3); attested in Sui Shu.
b_dingyuan.etymology_analysis: Military-administrative name meaning 'Pacifying the Distant Frontier', established by the Southern Liang dynasty along the Huai River borderlands in 504 CE.

b_zhaoyi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Zhaoyi County (招义县) under Northern Zhou (c. 579 CE, renamed from Suiling), later Huaming, and restored to Zhaoyi County in Tang under Haozhou; attested in Yuanhe Junxian Zhi and Xin Tang Shu.
b_zhaoyi.etymology_analysis: Means 'Summoning to Righteousness', a Northern Zhou / Tang frontier county name under Haozhou (renamed Zhaoxin in Song 976 CE).

b_liyang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Liyang County (历阳县) under Jiujiang Commandery in the Qin dynasty (c. 221 BCE); attested in Shi Ji and Han Shu.

morphemes.translation: north bank of river / sunny south slope

b_liyang.etymology_analysis: Topographic locator compound meaning 'North of the Li River (历水)' (or south of Mount Li), dating back to the Qin dynasty.

b_hanshan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Hanshan County (含山县) in 623 CE (Tang, Wude 6) from western Liyang County; restored in 704 CE (Chang'an 4) and attested in Xin Tang Shu.
b_hanshan.etymology_analysis: Named directly after Mount Han (含山) 30 li west of the county seat, described in gazetteers as peaks standing in array as if enclosing the basin.

b_hefei.first_mention_attestation: Established as Hefei County (合肥县) in the early Western Han (c. 202 BCE, or Qin dynasty); attested in Shi Ji and Han Shu.
b_hefei.etymology_analysis: Named after the confluence (合) of the East Fei and South Fei rivers (淝水), recorded since the Han dynasty.

b_shen.first_mention_attestation: Established as Shen County (慎县) in the Liu Song dynasty (420–479 CE) in modern Feidong County, Anhui; attested in Song Shu, Sui Shu, and Tang-era Luzhou records (birthplace of Bao Zheng in Song).
b_shen.etymology_analysis: Named after the earlier Han-dynasty Shen County (in Yingshang) via Southern Dynasties migrant-county (qiaozhi) naming; retained under Luzhou in Sui and Tang.

b_lujiang.first_mention_attestation: Lujiang County (庐江县) established in 583 CE (Sui, Kaihuang 3), named after Western Han Lujiang Commandery (121 BCE) and the Lu River; attested in Sui Shu.
b_lujiang.etymology_analysis: Named after the ancient Lu River (庐江, a Yangtze tributary) via the Western Han Lujiang Commandery (121 BCE).

b_chao.first_mention_attestation: Chao County (巢县) established in 624 CE (Tang, Wude 7) by merging Kaicheng and Fuyang; preceded on the same site by the Zhou-era State of Chao (巢国) and Qin/Han Juchao County (居巢县).
b_chao.etymology_analysis: Derived from the ancient Zhou-era State of Chao (巢国) and Qin/Han Juchao County (居巢), later shortened to Chao County in 624 CE.

b_shucheng_1.first_mention_attestation: Established as Shucheng County (舒城县) in 735 CE (Tang, Kaiyuan 23) from Hefei and Lujiang; Jiu Tang Shu notes it took its name from ancient Longshu County (龙舒县) and the Zhou-era Shu states.
b_shucheng_1.etymology_analysis: Named 'Walled City of Shu' after the Western Zhou / Spring and Autumn Qunshu (群舒) states and Han-era Longshu County.

b_shouchun.first_mention_attestation: In 241 BCE (King Kaolie 22), the State of Chu moved its capital east to Shouchun (寿春); established as Shouchun County by Qin in 223 BCE and attested in Shi Ji.
b_shouchun.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Chu-era capital name meaning 'Longevity and Springtime', serving as the last capital of Chu (241–223 BCE) and later seat of Shouzhou.

b_luan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Lu'an Kingdom (六安国) in 121 BCE (Western Han, Yuanshou 2) by Emperor Wu of Han, named after the ancient State of Lu (六国); attested in Han Shu.
b_luan.etymology_analysis: Named by Emperor Wu of Han in 121 BCE meaning 'May Lu be Pacified' (六安), after the ancient Spring and Autumn State of Lu (六国); the repo's 陆安 reflects the phonetic pronunciation Lù.

b_houqiu.first_mention_attestation: Established as Huoqiu County (霍丘县) in 599 CE (Sui, Kaihuang 19) under Shouzhou; attested in Sui Shu and Xin Tang Shu.
b_houqiu.etymology_analysis: Named after a local mound/hill associated with the ancient Huo/Liao area in western Anhui, established as a county in 599 CE.

b_anfeng.first_mention_attestation: Established as Anfeng County (安丰县) under Jiujiang Commandery in the Qin dynasty (c. 221 BCE), attested in Han Shu and Shui Jing Zhu; remained a county of Shouzhou in Sui and Tang.
b_anfeng.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Qin-Han agricultural name meaning 'Peace and Abundance', located near the ancient Quebei (Anfengtang) irrigation reservoir.

b_huoshan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Huoshan County (霍山县) in 583 CE (Sui, Kaihuang 3) by renaming Yue'an County; attested in Sui Shu and Xin Tang Shu.
b_huoshan.etymology_analysis: Named directly after Mount Huo (霍山, historically also Mount Tianzhu / Southern Marchmount), a prominent peak in the Dabie Mountains.

b_huaining.first_mention_attestation: Established as Huaining County (怀宁县) during the Eastern Jin Yixi era (405–418 CE) under Jinxi Commandery on the site of ancient Wan County; attested in Song Shu.
b_huaining.etymology_analysis: Means 'Cherishing Tranquility' (or pacifying the Man-Zuo peoples of the Dabie foothills), established in the Eastern Jin Yixi era.

b_tongcheng.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Tongcheng County (桐城县) in 757 CE (Tang, Zhide 2) from Tong'an County to avoid the character 'An' (安) due to An Lushan's rebellion; attested in Xin Tang Shu.
b_tongcheng.etymology_analysis: Named 'Walled City of Tong' after the Spring and Autumn State of Tong (桐国) and Tongxiang, adopted in 757 CE when 'An' was tabooed.

b_taihu.first_mention_attestation: Established as Taihu Zuo County (太湖左县) in 448 CE (Liu Song, Yuanjia 25) under Jinxi Commandery; attested in Song Shu and Taiping Huanyu Ji.
b_taihu.etymology_analysis: Named after the local Taihu water/lake beside Mount Long (龙山太湖水) in southwestern Anhui, not the larger Lake Tai in Jiangsu.

b_susong.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Susong County (宿松县) in 598 CE (Sui, Kaihuang 18) from Gaotang/Songzi; attested in Sui Shu and Xin Tang Shu.
b_susong.etymology_analysis: Means 'Old Song(zi)', referencing the earlier Eastern Jin / Han-era Songzi County (松滋县) located in the area.

b_wangjiang.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Wangjiang County (望江县) in 598 CE (Sui, Kaihuang 18) from Yixiang County (originally Xinye, est. 405 CE); attested in Sui Shu and Xin Tang Shu.
b_wangjiang.etymology_analysis: Directional/view name meaning 'Gazing at the Yangtze River', reflecting the county's position on the northern bank of the Yangtze.

b_chen.first_mention_attestation: Established as Chen County (郴县) in the Qin dynasty (221 BCE), later seat of Guiyang Commandery and place of exile of Emperor Yi of Chu in 206 BCE; attested in Shi Ji and Han Shu.

morphemes.translation: Chen (place name; phono-semantic 林 + 邑 'settlement in the woods')

b_chen.etymology_analysis: Ancient Qin-Han settlement name uniquely coined for this southern Hunan basin, combining 林 (forest) and 邑 (settlement).

b_zixing.first_mention_attestation: Established as Zixing County (资兴县) in 672 CE (Tang, Xianheng 3), succeeding Eastern Han Hanning County (136 CE) and Sui Jinxing County; attested in Xin Tang Shu.
b_zixing.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Tang-era county name meaning 'Prospering Through Resources', formed in 672 CE on the older Hanning/Jinxing county territory.

b_yongxing_1.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Yongxing County (永兴县) in 1073 CE (Northern Song, Xining 6) upon the recommendation of Chenzhou Prefect Li Shixie, replacing Tang-era Gaoting County; attested in Song Shi.
b_yongxing_1.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Northern Song name meaning 'Eternal Prosperity', bestowed in 1073 CE when Gaoting County was renamed.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Han Shu (Book of Han) and Xin Tang Shu: Bian County (202 BCE), later Anling (725 CE) and Gaoting (742 CE).
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally Bian County (便县, est. 202 BCE); re-established as Anling County in 725 CE and renamed Gaoting County in 742 CE before becoming Yongxing in 1073 CE.

b_gaoting.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Gaoting County (高亭县) in 742 CE (Tang, Tianbao 1) from Anling County (which had been split from Chen County in 725 CE); attested in Xin Tang Shu.
b_gaoting.etymology_analysis: Means 'High Post/Pavilion', the Tang-era name (742–1073 CE) for modern Yongxing County in Chenzhou.

b_yizhang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yizhang County (义章县) in 617 CE (Sui, Daye 13) by splitting southern Chen County; attested in Xin Tang Shu (renamed Yizhang 宜章 in 976 CE to avoid Song Taizong's taboo name).
b_yizhang.etymology_analysis: Named after the Zhang River (章水) and 'righteousness' (义); in 976 CE (Song Taiping Xingguo 1), 义 was replaced by 宜 due to Zhao Kuangyi's naming taboo.

b_pingyang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Pingyang County (平阳县) and Pingyang Commandery in 315 CE (Western Jin, Jianxing 3), split from Chen County; seat of Chenzhou from 758 CE; attested in Jin Shu and Xin Tang Shu.

morphemes.translation: sunny south slope / north of river

b_pingyang.etymology_analysis: Topographic/auspicious -yang compound meaning 'Level Sunny Slope', the Jin-through-Tang county name for Guiyang County in Hunan.

b_lanshan.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Lanshan County (蓝山县) in 742 CE (Tang, Tianbao 1) from Nanping County (originally Western Han); attested in Xin Tang Shu.
b_lanshan.etymology_analysis: Named directly after Mount Lan (蓝山, 'Indigo Mountain') in the Nanling range of southern Hunan.

b_linwu.first_mention_attestation: Established as Linwu County (临武县) in 202 BCE (Western Han, Gaozu 5) under Guiyang Commandery; attested in Han Shu.
b_linwu.etymology_analysis: Locator compound meaning 'Overlooking the Wu River (武水)', a headwater tributary of the Pearl River system.

b_hengyang_1.first_mention_attestation: Hengyang County (衡阳县) established in 589 CE (Sui, Kaihuang 9) by merging Linzheng, Zhong'an, and Xincheng counties as seat of Hengzhou; preceded by Eastern Wu Hengyang Commandery (257 CE). Attested in Sui Shu.
b_hengyang_1.etymology_analysis: Directional -yang compound meaning 'South of Mount Heng' (衡山之南).

b_chaling.first_mention_attestation: Established as Chaling County (茶陵县) in 202 BCE (Western Han, Gaozu 5) under the Changsha Kingdom; attested in Han Shu and Hou Han Shu.
b_chaling.etymology_analysis: Means 'Tea Hill' (originally written 荼陵 in Han Shu), referring to the tea-growing hills of eastern Hunan.

b_you.first_mention_attestation: Established as You County (攸县) in 202 BCE (Western Han, Gaozu 5) under the Changsha Kingdom; attested in Han Shu and Shui Jing Zhu.
b_you.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the You Stream/River (攸溪 / 攸水) flowing past the county seat, as noted in Shui Jing Zhu.

b_changning.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Changning County (常宁县) in 742 CE (Tang, Tianbao 1) from Xinning County (originally split from Leiyang in 257 CE); attested in Xin Tang Shu.
b_changning.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Tang-dynasty name meaning 'Enduring Peace', bestowed in 742 CE when Xinning County was renamed.

b_leiyang.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Leiyang County (耒阳县) in 202 BCE (Western Han, Gaozu 5) from Qin-dynasty Lei County (221 BCE); attested in Han Shu.

morphemes.translation: north bank of river / sunny side

b_leiyang.etymology_analysis: Locator -yang compound meaning 'North of the Lei River (耒水)', dating back to 202 BCE.

b_guiyang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Guiyang County (桂阳县) in 206 BCE (early Western Han, modern Lianzhou in northern Guangdong, matching c_lianzhou); attested in Han Shu.

morphemes.translation: sunny south slope / north of river

b_guiyang.etymology_analysis: Locator -yang compound meaning 'North of the Gui River (桂水)', the Han-through-Tang county seat of Lianzhou (连州).

b_lianshan.first_mention_attestation: Sui Renshou 1st year (601 CE): Guangze County (formerly Liang-era Guangde County) was renamed Lianshan County to avoid the naming taboo of Crown Prince Yang Guang.
b_lianshan.etymology_analysis: Named in 601 CE for the interlocking mountain ranges of the Nanling highlands in northwestern Guangdong.

b_yangshan.first_mention_attestation: Western Han Yuanding 6th year (111 BCE): Emperor Wu of Han formally established Yangshan County following a late-Qin military camp (Yangshan Pass).
b_yangshan.etymology_analysis: Derived from the sunny southern slopes of the Nanling mountains flanking the Lian River valley.

b_changsha.first_mention_attestation: Qin dynasty (221 BCE): Changsha Commandery established after Qin conquered Chu; the name Changsha is also attested in late Zhou/Warring States Chu records.
b_changsha.etymology_analysis: Traditionally explained either as a descriptive name for the long sandbars in the Xiang River (such as Orange Isle) or from the Changsha star-field correspondence.

b_xiangtan.first_mention_attestation: Southern Liang Tianjian era (502–519 CE): Xiangtan County was first carved from Yinshan County; in Tang Tianbao 8th year (749 CE), Xiangxi County was renamed Xiangtan and seated at Luokou.
b_xiangtan.etymology_analysis: Compound of the Xiang River and a deep river pool (Zhaotan), referring to the deep bend of the Xiang River at the settlement.

b_liuyang.first_mention_attestation: Eastern Han Jian'an 14th year (209 CE): Sun Quan split Linxiang to establish Liuyang (written 刘阳, standardized to 浏阳 in 420 CE and restored under Tang in 708 CE).
b_liuyang.etymology_analysis: Toponymic '-yang' compound denoting a settlement located on the sunny northern bank of the Liuyang River.

b_xiangxiang.first_mention_attestation: Western Han Jianping 4th year (3 BCE): Emperor Ai of Han enfeoffed Changsha Prince Liu Chang as Marquis of Xiangxiang, which was later converted into Xiangxiang County.
b_xiangxiang.etymology_analysis: Derived from its location in the Xiang River basin (specifically along the Lian River tributary), designating a township of the Xiang region.

b_hengshan.first_mention_attestation: Western Jin Yongxi 1st year (290 CE): Hengyang County (created 257 CE) was renamed Hengshan County; Mount Heng itself is attested in the Book of Documents (Shangshu).
b_hengshan.etymology_analysis: Directly named after the sacred Mount Heng (Southern Sacred Peak), one of China's Five Great Mountains.

b_hongdao.first_mention_attestation: Tang Tianbao 6th year (747 CE): Yingdao County (seat of Daozhou) was renamed Hongdao County, which remained its name through 867 CE until Song times.
b_hongdao.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Tang-era renaming of Yingdao County, echoing both the Confucian/Daoist ideal of magnifying the Way and the prefecture name Daozhou.

b_dali.first_mention_attestation: Tang Dali 2nd year (767 CE): Dali County was split from Yantang County under Daozhou, named after Emperor Daizong's Dali reign era.
b_dali.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Dali reign era (766–779 CE) of Emperor Daizong of Tang when the county was established in 767 CE.

b_jianghua.first_mention_attestation: Tang Wude 4th year (621 CE): Jianghua County was split from Fengcheng County under Yingzhou/Daozhou.
b_jianghua.etymology_analysis: Tang-era auspicious county name referring to the scenic river valleys (Tuo and Xiao headwaters) of southernmost Hunan.

b_xiangyuan_1.first_mention_attestation: Sui Kaihuang 9th year (589 CE): Taoyang and Lingling counties were merged to form Xiangyuan County, which served as the seat until renamed Qingxiang in 939 CE.
b_xiangyuan_1.etymology_analysis: Compound of the Xiang River and 'yuan' (headwaters), reflecting its position near the upper reaches of the Xiang River system.

b_xiyan.first_mention_attestation: Early Northern Song dynasty (c. 960 CE): The area was first designated Xiyan (西延) under Quanzhou.
b_xiyan.etymology_analysis: Song-era regional name Xiyan (westward extension of Quanzhou) in the mountainous borderland between Guangxi and Hunan.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Han Shu), Treatise on Geography (Western Han Yuanding 6th year, 111 BCE, as Fuyi/Taoyang under Lingling Commandery)
older_name_by_867.notes: In Qin-Han times the area was known as Fuyi (扶夷) and fell under Taoyang County (111 BCE) and later Sui-Tang Xiangyuan County (589 CE) before being named Xiyan in the early Northern Song.

b_guanyang.first_mention_attestation: Sui Daye 13th year (617 CE): Guanyang County was established (restoring/renaming the older Western Han Guanyin County of 168 BCE).
b_guanyang.etymology_analysis: Toponymic '-yang' compound named for its position along the Guan River in northeastern Guangxi.

b_shaoyang.first_mention_attestation: Western Jin Taikang 1st year (280 CE): Zhaoyang County (formerly Western Han Zhaoyang Marquisate, 5 CE) was renamed Shaoyang County to avoid the naming taboo of Sima Zhao.
b_shaoyang.etymology_analysis: Toponymic '-yang' compound on the north bank of the Shao River, modified from Zhaoyang in 280 CE due to Jin imperial naming taboo.

b_xinhua.first_mention_attestation: Northern Song Xining 5th year (1072 CE): Xinhua County was founded following the Song pacification of the Meishan region.
b_xinhua.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Northern Song phrase 'xinjin guihua' (newly submitted to imperial civilization) after the 1072 CE Meishan campaign.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Western Jin Taikang-era Gaoping County (280 CE) and Sui-Tang Meishan indigenous territory records
older_name_by_867.notes: Before the 1072 CE Northern Song establishment of Xinhua County, the region was known as Meishan (梅山) and parts had earlier belonged to Western Jin Gaoping County (280 CE) and Tang Shaoyang/Yiyang jurisdictions.

b_anhua_1.first_mention_attestation: Northern Song Xining 5th year (1072 CE): Anhua County was founded alongside Xinhua after the pacification of the Meishan peoples.
b_anhua_1.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Song pacification motto 'min an de hua' (tranquility for the people transformed by virtue) in 1072 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Han Shu), Treatise on Geography (Western Han Yiyang County, c. 202 BCE) and Tang-era Meishan
older_name_by_867.notes: Prior to the 1072 CE Northern Song establishment of Anhua County, the area formed part of the Meishan indigenous region and earlier Han-Tang Yiyang County.

b_wugang.first_mention_attestation: Three Kingdoms Eastern Wu (c. 266 CE): Han-era Liangxian County was renamed Wugang County after Mount Wugang; restored under Tang in 621 CE.
b_wugang.etymology_analysis: Named after the local Mount Wugang ridge, combining 'martial' and 'ridge' in reference to its strategic terrain.

b_suining.first_mention_attestation: Northern Song Chongning 2nd year (1103 CE): Shizhu County (established 1081 CE) was reestablished and renamed Suining County.
b_suining.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Song administrative phrase 'sui zhi yi ning' (pacify in order to achieve tranquility) in 1103 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Han Shu) (Western Han Fuyi Marquisate, 124 BCE) and Tang Wugang County records
older_name_by_867.notes: Before the Song establishment of Shizhu (1081 CE) and Suining (1103 CE), the area was part of Han Fuyi Marquisate/County and Sui-Tang Wugang County.

b_xinning.first_mention_attestation: Southern Song Shaoxing 25th year (1155 CE): Xinning County was established under Wugang Commandery.
b_xinning.etymology_analysis: Song-era auspicious county name meaning 'newly pacified / tranquil' upon its creation in 1155 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Han Shu) (Western Han Fuyi Marquisate, 124 BCE) and Tang Wugang County
older_name_by_867.notes: The site was originally Han Fuyi (夫彝) Marquisate/County (124 BCE), later merged into Wugang County until Southern Song Xinning County was created in 1155 CE.

b_lingling.first_mention_attestation: Qin dynasty (221–206 BCE): Lingling County was established; in 111 BCE, Han Emperor Wu founded Lingling Commandery.
b_lingling.etymology_analysis: Ancient Qin-Han toponym of southern Hunan, traditionally linked to the Jiuyi mountains or Shun's tumulus.

b_qiyang.first_mention_attestation: Three Kingdoms Eastern Wu (257/268 CE): Qiyang County was split from Quanling County; merged in Sui and restored in Tang Wude 4th year (621 CE).
b_qiyang.etymology_analysis: Toponymic '-yang' compound named for its location on the sunny southern side of Mount Qi (祁山).

b_dongan.first_mention_attestation: Northern Song Yongxi 1st year (984 CE): Dong'an Field was elevated to Dong'an County, carved out of Lingling County.
b_dongan.etymology_analysis: Song-era county name 'Eastern Peace', upgraded from a local military/fiscal station (Dong'an Field) in 984 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Han Shu), Treatise on Geography (Western Han Quanling County, 111 BCE; Sui-Tang Lingling County, 589 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Dong'an was carved out of Lingling County (formerly Han Quanling County) in 984 CE.

b_jinling.first_mention_attestation: Western Jin Yongxing 2nd year (305 CE): Piling Commandery and County were renamed Jinling due to imperial naming taboo; Jinling served as the seat of Changzhou in Tang.
b_jinling.etymology_analysis: Renamed from Piling (毗陵) to Jinling in 305 CE to honor the Jin dynasty while avoiding Sima Pi's naming taboo.

b_wuxi.first_mention_attestation: Western Han (202 BCE): Wuxi County was formally established after ancient tin deposits in the area were exhausted.
b_wuxi.etymology_analysis: Literally 'Without Tin', referring to the depletion of local tin mines around Mount Xi by the early Han dynasty.

b_yixing.first_mention_attestation: Western Jin Yongjia 4th year (310 CE): Yixing Commandery was created in recognition of Zhou Qi's military achievements; later Yixing County in Sui-Tang.
b_yixing.etymology_analysis: Commemorative Western Jin name ('Righteousness Rising') honoring the loyalty of local aristocrat Zhou Qi and his clan.

b_jiangyin.first_mention_attestation: Liang/Chen transition (557 CE): Jiangyin County was created from Jinling (formerly Piling) as the seat of Jiangyin Commandery.
b_jiangyin.etymology_analysis: Toponymic '-yin' compound denoting its position on the southern bank of the lower Yangtze River.

b_jiangning.first_mention_attestation: Western Jin Taikang 2nd year (281 CE): Jiangning County was established southwest of Jianye (modern Nanjing).
b_jiangning.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Jin-era county name meaning 'Tranquil Yangtze' after the Western Jin pacification of Eastern Wu.

b_gourong.first_mention_attestation: Western Han Yuanshuo 1st year (129 BCE): Liu Dang was enfeoffed as Marquis of Jurong, and the fief became Jurong County the following year (128 BCE).
b_gourong.etymology_analysis: Derived from the nearby Gouqu Mountains (Maoshan), whose curved ridges enclose the valley.

b_dangtu.first_mention_attestation: Sui Kaihuang 9th year (589 CE): Dangtu County was established at Gushu (modern Dangtu, Anhui), transplanting the earlier Qin-Han Dangtu name.
b_dangtu.etymology_analysis: Originally named after Mount Tu on the Huai River and transplanted south to Gushu on the Yangtze during the Sui reorganization in 589 CE.

b_lishui.first_mention_attestation: Sui Kaihuang 11th year (591 CE): Lishui County was established south of Nanjing, named after the Li River.
b_lishui.etymology_analysis: Directly named after the Li River (Lishui), a major waterway in southern Jiangsu.

b_dantu.first_mention_attestation: Qin Shi Huang 37th year (210 BCE): Guyang was renamed Dantu during the First Emperor's eastern tour.
b_dantu.etymology_analysis: Named in 210 BCE for the 3,000 red-clad convict laborers (zheyi tu) ordered by Qin Shi Huang to excavate Jingxian Mountain.

b_danyang.first_mention_attestation: Tang Tianbao 1st year (742 CE): Qu'e County (formerly Qin-Han Qu'e/Yunyang) was renamed Danyang County after the Han commandery name.
b_danyang.etymology_analysis: Toponymic '-yang' compound adopted from the ancient Danyang Commandery name in 742 CE, originally referencing red-earth hills.

b_jintan.first_mention_attestation: Tang Chuigong 4th year (688 CE): Former Jinshan County was reestablished as Jintan County, named after Jintan Hill on Mount Mao.
b_jintan.etymology_analysis: Named in 688 CE after Jintan ('Golden Altar'), a Daoist peak/site on nearby Mount Mao, to distinguish it from Jinshan in Zhejiang.

b_wu.first_mention_attestation: Qin dynasty (221 BCE): Wu County was established as the seat of Kuaiji Commandery, continuing the ancient Spring and Autumn state name Wu.
b_wu.etymology_analysis: Bare choronym of the ancient State of Wu and the core Wu region centered on Suzhou.

b_kunshang.first_mention_attestation: Southern Liang Datong 2nd year (536 CE): Kunshan County was established, named after Mount Kun (Kunshan).
b_kunshang.etymology_analysis: Directly named after Mount Kun (Kunshan), an isolated hill in the eastern Yangtze Delta.

b_changshu.first_mention_attestation: Southern Liang Datong 6th year (540 CE): Changshu became an independent county.
b_changshu.etymology_analysis: Auspicious agricultural name meaning 'constantly ripe/abundant harvests', reflecting the fertile Yangtze Delta plains.

b_qiupu.first_mention_attestation: Sui Kaihuang 19th year (599 CE): Qiupu County was established on the site of Han Shicheng; it served as Chizhou's seat through the Tang dynasty.
b_qiupu.etymology_analysis: Toponymic '-pu' compound named for the Qiupu River estuary where it meets the Yangtze.

b_qingyang.first_mention_attestation: Tang Tianbao 1st year (742 CE): Qingyang County was newly established from parts of Jing, Nanling, and Qiupu counties.
b_qingyang.etymology_analysis: Toponymic '-yang' compound named for its location on the sunny southern side of Mount Qing (青山).

b_shidai.first_mention_attestation: Southern Liang Datong 2nd year (536 CE): Shidai County was established; later restored under Tang in Yongtai 2nd year (766 CE) under Chizhou.
b_shidai.etymology_analysis: Descriptive compound referring to natural stone formations across the Qiupu River resembling a stone dam or weir.

b_zhide.first_mention_attestation: Tang Zhide 2nd year (757 CE): Zhide County was split from Qiupu and Poyang counties and named after Emperor Suzong's Zhide reign era.
b_zhide.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Zhide reign era (756–758 CE) of Emperor Suzong of Tang upon its founding in 757 CE.

b_guangde.first_mention_attestation: Eastern Han Jian'an period (c. 200 CE): Sun Ce split Guzhang County to establish Guangde County.
b_guangde.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Eastern Han county name meaning 'vast virtue / imperial grace'.

b_jianping.first_mention_attestation: Northern Song Duangong 1st year (988 CE): Five northwestern townships of Guangde County were split off to establish Jianping County.
b_jianping.etymology_analysis: Northern Song auspicious county name ('Establish Peace') given in 988 CE, later renamed Langxi in 1914.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Eastern Han Jian'an period records of Guangde County (c. 200 CE), carved from Qin-Han Guzhang County
older_name_by_867.notes: Prior to 988 CE, the territory of Jianping (modern Langxi) formed the northwestern townships of Guangde County (est. c. 200 CE).

b_jixi.first_mention_attestation: Tang Dali 11th year (776 CE): Jixi County was formally established in the Huizhou/Shezhou region.
b_jixi.etymology_analysis: Named in 776 CE for the local Jixi brook, whose winding currents were likened to spun hemp.

b_xiuning.first_mention_attestation: Sui Kaihuang 18th year (598 CE): Haining County (originally Eastern Han Xiuyang/Haiyang, 208 CE) was renamed Xiuning County.
b_xiuning.etymology_analysis: Sui-era auspicious renaming of Haining County in 598 CE, combining 'xiu' (blessing/rest) and 'ning' (tranquility).

b_wuyaun.first_mention_attestation: Established as Wuyuan County (婺源县) in 740 CE (Tang Kaiyuan 28) under Shezhou.
b_wuyaun.etymology_analysis: Named in 740 CE for the source/headwaters (源) of the Wushui/Wu River under the astrological division of the Wunu (婺女) star.

b_qimen.first_mention_attestation: Established as Qimen County (祁门县) in 766 CE (Tang Yongtai 2) under Shezhou.
b_qimen.etymology_analysis: Named in 766 CE after Mount Qi (祁山) to the northeast and the rocky river-gate (阊门) of the Chang River to the southwest.

b_she_1.first_mention_attestation: Established as She County (歙县) under the Qin dynasty (221 BCE); later seat of Xin'an Commandery and Sui-Tang Shezhou.
b_she_1.etymology_analysis: Ancient Qin-dynasty county name (歙), traditionally associated with the Shepu (歙浦) watercourse south of the walled town.

b_xuancheng.first_mention_attestation: Xuancheng Commandery (宣城郡) was established in 281 CE (Western Jin Taikang 2), and Wanling County was renamed Xuancheng County (宣城县) in 607 CE (Sui Daye 3).
b_xuancheng.etymology_analysis: Auspicious administrative name meaning 'Proclaimed City' (宣城), adopted for the commandery in 281 CE and the county seat in 607 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Geographical Treatise), Western Han Yuanfeng 2 (109 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Seat of Danyang Commandery from 109 BCE; renamed Xuancheng County in 607 CE.

b_ningguo.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 208 CE (Eastern Han Jian'an 13) when Sun Quan split the southern part of Wanling County into Ningguo County (宁国县).
b_ningguo.etymology_analysis: Derived from the classical Yijing phrase 'all states are tranquil' (万国咸宁), expressing pacification of the Shanyue frontier.

b_jing.first_mention_attestation: Jing County (泾县) was established in the Qin/early Western Han period and is attested in the Book of Han (109 BCE split of Lingyang from Jing County).
b_jing.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the local Jing Creek/River (泾溪/泾水) in southern Anhui (unrelated to the Shaanxi Jing River noted in the repo's calque).

b_jingde.first_mention_attestation: Established as Jingde County (旌德县) in 763 CE (Tang Baoying 2; recorded as 765/766 CE in some Tang gazetteers) under Xuanzhou.
b_jingde.etymology_analysis: Auspicious moralizing name ('Commend Virtue', 旌表其礼以彰其德) bestowed after suppressing a local Tang rebellion.

b_nanling.first_mention_attestation: Established as Nanling County and Nanling Commandery (南陵县/郡) in 525 CE (Southern Liang Putong 6).
b_nanling.etymology_analysis: Directional/topographic compound ('South Hill'), transplanted from the Han county name Nanling in Guanzhong via Eastern Jin émigré garrison (南陵戍).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Geographical Treatise)
older_name_by_867.notes: Western Han Chungu County (109 BCE) encompassed the area before Nanling was established in 525 CE.

b_duchang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Duchang County (都昌县) in 622 CE (Tang Wude 5) under Haozhou, later Jiangzhou.
b_duchang.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Tang-era county name ('Great Prosperity') formed when carving out the northern shore of Poyang Lake in 622 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Geographical Treatise)
older_name_by_867.notes: Han-era Qiaoyang County (201 BCE, abolished 421 CE) lay in the Duchang territory.

b_pengze.first_mention_attestation: Established as Pengze County (彭泽县) in 201 BCE (Western Han Gaozu 6) under Yuzhang Commandery.
b_pengze.etymology_analysis: Named directly after Pengli Marsh (彭蠡泽, abbreviated 彭泽), the ancient name for the Poyang Lake basin.

b_hukou.first_mention_attestation: Established as Hukou County (湖口县) in 938 CE (Southern Tang Shengyuan 2), split from Pengze County.
b_hukou.etymology_analysis: Topographic compound meaning 'Lake Mouth', referring to the outlet where Poyang Lake empties into the Yangtze River.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Liu Song garrison (湖口戍, 420-479 CE) under Pengze County (201 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Hukou Garrison existed from Liu Song (420-479 CE) under Pengze County before becoming an independent county in 938 CE.

b_poyang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Fan County (番县) in 221 BCE (Qin dynasty), renamed Fanyang (番阳) in Western Han and Poyang (鄱阳) in Eastern Han; earlier Chu town of Po (番).
b_poyang.etymology_analysis: Locator compound ('South of Mount Po' or Po River), evolving from Chu's Po (番) to Han-era Poyang (鄱阳).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Spring and Autumn Chu settlement Po (番), Qin Fan County (221 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Earlier orthography 番/番阳 before 鄱阳.

b_fuliang.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Fuliang County (浮梁县) in 742 CE (Tang Tianbao 1) from Xinchang County (新昌县).
b_fuliang.etymology_analysis: Literally 'Floating Bridge' (pontoon bridge across the Chang River; note the repo's calque mistakenly rendered 梁 as 'Liang Dynasty').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Tang Kaiyuan 4 (716 CE) Xinchang County
older_name_by_867.notes: Renamed Fuliang in 742 CE and moved to its current site in 817 CE after floods.

b_dexing.first_mention_attestation: Established as Dexing County (德兴县) in 938 CE (Southern Tang Shengyuan 2), upgrading Denggong Chang (邓公场).
b_dexing.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Southern Tang name from the motto 'treasures of mountains and rivers flourish only through virtue' (山川之宝，惟德乃兴).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Eastern Han Guanghe 1 (178 CE) Leping seat at Yinchengfan; Chen silver mine
older_name_by_867.notes: Yincheng (Silver City) was the original 178 CE seat of Leping County before Dexing was split off in 938 CE.

b_yugan_2.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yugan County (余干县) in 221 BCE (Qin Shi Huang 26), written Yuhan (余汗) in Han.
b_yugan_2.etymology_analysis: Ancient Qin-Han county name (余干 / 余汗), likely preserving a Baiyue substrate toponym associated with the Yu River (余水).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Geographical Treatise)
older_name_by_867.notes: Han-era orthography 余汗 for the same county.

b_leping_1.first_mention_attestation: Originally founded as Le'an County (乐安县) in 178 CE (Eastern Han Guanghe 1), renamed Leping County (乐平县) in 621 CE (Tang Wude 4).
b_leping_1.etymology_analysis: Combines the Le'an River (乐安江) to the south and Pinglin (平林) forest to the north, also carrying an auspicious 'joyful peace' meaning.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Eastern Han Guanghe 1 (178 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Founded in 178 CE as Le'an County; renamed Leping in 621 CE.

b_shangrao.first_mention_attestation: Established as Shangrao County (上饶县) in the late Eastern Han Jian'an era (c. 196-204 CE), and re-established in 758 CE (Tang Qianyuan 1) as seat of Xinzhou.
b_shangrao.etymology_analysis: Directional/laudatory compound meaning 'Upper Abundance' (山郁珍奇、上等富饶), referring to its upland location relative to Raozhou.

b_yushan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yushan County (玉山县) in 695 CE (Wu Zhou Zhengsheng 1) under Quzhou, later Xinzhou.
b_yushan.etymology_analysis: Named directly after Mount Yu / Huaiyu Mountain (怀玉山/玉山) within its territory.

b_guixi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Guixi County (贵溪县) in 765 CE (Tang Yongtai 1) under Xinzhou.
b_guixi.etymology_analysis: Named directly after Gui Creek (贵溪), at whose mouth (贵溪口) the Tang county seat was founded in 765 CE.

b_yiyang_1.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Yiyang County (弋阳县) in 592 CE (Sui Kaihuang 12) when the county seat moved north of the Yi River.

morphemes.translation: north bank of a river (sunny side)

b_yiyang_1.etymology_analysis: Hydronymic locator compound meaning 'North Bank of the Yi River' (弋水之阳), replacing the older name Geyang in 592 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Eastern Han Jian'an 15 (210 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally founded as Geyang County in 210 CE; relocated and renamed Yiyang in 592 CE.

b_yanshan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yanshan County (铅山县) in 953 CE (Southern Tang Baoda 11), split from Yiyang and Shangrao.
b_yanshan.etymology_analysis: Named directly after Mount Yan (铅山, 'Lead Mountain'), 4 li west of Yongping, which yielded lead and copper ores (site of a Tang-era mining yard 铅山场).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Sui Kaihuang 12 (592 CE) Yiyang; Tang Qianyuan 1 (758 CE) Shangrao
older_name_by_867.notes: Territory belonged to Yiyang and Shangrao (with a Tang mining yard 铅山场) before county elevation in 953 CE.

b_xunyang.first_mention_attestation: Xunyang County (寻阳县) was first attested in 164 BCE north of the Yangtze and re-established on the south bank at modern Jiujiang in 589 CE (Sui Kaihuang 9), written 浔阳县 in Tang (621 CE).
b_xunyang.etymology_analysis: Hydronymic locator compound meaning 'North of the Xun River' (浔水之阳), referring to Xunyang (浔阳) in Jiujiang, Jiangxi.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Geographical Treatise)
older_name_by_867.notes: Han-era Chaisang County and Pencheng were merged into Xunyang County in 589 CE.

b_ruichang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Ruichang County (瑞昌县) in 939 CE (Southern Tang Shengyuan 3), upgrading Chiwu Chang (赤乌场).

morphemes.translation: auspicious omen (of the red crow 赤乌之瑞)

b_ruichang.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Southern Tang name referencing the Eastern Wu legend of an auspicious red crow ('瑞应武昌'), upgrading Tang-era Chiwu Chang.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Tang Jianzhong 4 (783 CE), split from Xunyang
older_name_by_867.notes: Established as Chiwu Chang in 783 CE; elevated to Ruichang County in 939 CE.

b_dean.first_mention_attestation: Established as De'an County (德安县) in 927 CE (Yang Wu Shunyi 7), upgrading Putang Chang (蒲塘场).
b_dean.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Five Dynasties name meaning 'Pacified by Virtue' (德所绥安), bestowed when Putang Chang was elevated to a county in 927 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Geographical Treatise)
older_name_by_867.notes: Western Han Liling County (renamed Puting under Wang Mang) occupied the site prior to Putang Chang and 927 CE De'an.

b_linchuan.first_mention_attestation: Linchuan Commandery (临川郡) was established in 257 CE (Eastern Wu Taiping 2), and Linru County was renamed Linchuan County (临川县) in 589 CE (Sui Kaihuang 9).
b_linchuan.etymology_analysis: Descriptive topographic compound meaning 'Overlooking the River', referring to its position along the Ru/Fu River.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Eastern Han Yongyuan 8 (96 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally founded as Linru County in 96 CE; renamed Linchuan County in 589 CE.

b_jinxi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Jinxi County (金溪县) in 994 CE (Northern Song Chunhua 5).
b_jinxi.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Jinxi ('Golden Stream'), known for Tang-era silver and gold mining/smelting sites.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Sui Kaihuang 9 (589 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Part of Linchuan County (with Tang-era silver smelting yards) prior to 994 CE.

b_yihuang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yihuang County (宜黄县) in 257 CE (Eastern Wu Taiping 2) under Linchuan Commandery (abolished in 589 CE and restored in 970 CE).
b_yihuang.etymology_analysis: Portmanteau hydronym named for the confluence of the Yi River (宜水) and Huang River (黄水).

b_chongren.first_mention_attestation: Established as Chongren County (崇仁县) in 589 CE (Sui Kaihuang 9) under Fuzhou, replacing Bashan County.
b_chongren.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Confucian moralizing name ('Exalt Benevolence') bestowed upon Sui unification in 589 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Eastern Wu Taiping 2 (257 CE) Xinjian; Liang Datong 2 (536 CE) Bashan
older_name_by_867.notes: Bashan County/Commandery (536 CE) and Xinjian County (257 CE) were merged into Chongren in 589 CE.

b_lean_1.first_mention_attestation: Established as Le'an County (乐安县) in 1149 CE (Southern Song Shaoxing 19), split from Chongren and Yongfeng.
b_lean_1.etymology_analysis: Named after Le'an Township (乐安乡), one of the four townships combined to form the county in 1149 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Sui Kaihuang 9 (589 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Territory belonged to Chongren County (589 CE) prior to 1149 CE.

b_nanchang.first_mention_attestation: Founded as Nanchang County (南昌县) in 202 BCE (Western Han Gaozu 5) by General Guan Ying as seat of Yuzhang Commandery.
b_nanchang.etymology_analysis: Auspicious directional compound meaning 'Prosperity of the South' (昌大南疆), coined upon Han establishment in 202 BCE.

b_wuning.first_mention_attestation: Established as Wuning County (武宁县) in 704 CE (Wu Zhou Chang'an 4), split from Jianchang County.
b_wuning.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Tang/Wu Zhou name ('Martial Tranquility'), seated at Xi'an-li (西安里) in 704 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Western Han Jingdi 3 (154 BCE) Haihun; Eastern Han Jian'an Xi'an
older_name_by_867.notes: Split from Haihun into Xi'an County in Eastern Han, later merged into Jianchang before becoming Wuning in 704 CE.

b_jianchang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Jianchang County (建昌县) in 154 CE (Eastern Han Yongxing 2); merged with Haihun in 425 CE.
b_jianchang.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Eastern Han name meaning 'Establish Prosperity'; renamed Yongxiu in 1914.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Western Han Gaozu 6 (201 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Haihun County (201 BCE) was merged into Jianchang County in 425 CE.

b_fengcheng.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Fengcheng County (丰城县) in 280 CE (Western Jin Taikang era) from Fucheng County (富城县).
b_fengcheng.etymology_analysis: Literally 'Abundant City' (also referencing the Feng River 丰水), renamed from Fucheng in 280 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Eastern Han Jian'an 15 (210 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Founded as Fucheng County in 210 CE; moved and renamed Fengcheng in 280 CE.

b_fenning.first_mention_attestation: Established as Fenning County (分宁县) in 800 CE (Tang Zhenyuan 16), split from Wuning County.
b_fenning.etymology_analysis: Administrative name meaning 'Split from (Wu)ning', coined when Xiba Township of Wuning County was made a separate county in 800 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Spring and Autumn Wu-Chu frontier settlement Ai (艾), Han Jian'ai
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Ai (艾) / Han Jian'ai lay in the territory before merging into Jianchang and Wuning.

b_nancheng.first_mention_attestation: Established as Nancheng County (南城县) in 202 BCE (Western Han Gaozu 5) under Yuzhang Commandery.
b_nancheng.etymology_analysis: Directional compound meaning 'South City', positioned south of the commandery seat Nanchang.

b_nanfeng.first_mention_attestation: Established as Nanfeng County (南丰县) in 257 CE (Eastern Wu Taiping 2), split from southern Nancheng County.
b_nanfeng.etymology_analysis: Originally named Feng County (丰县), prefixed with 'South' (南) to distinguish it from Feng County in Jiangsu.

b_guangchang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Guangchang County (广昌县) in 1138 CE (Southern Song Shaoxing 8), split from Nanfeng County.
b_guangchang.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Song-dynasty name ('Broad Prosperity'), reflecting its location at the broad headwaters of the Fu River.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Eastern Wu Taiping 2 (257 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Part of Nanfeng County prior to 1138 CE.

b_luling.first_mention_attestation: Established as Luling County (庐陵县) in 211 BCE (Qin Shi Huang 36; some sources cite 221 BCE) under Jiujiang Commandery.
b_luling.etymology_analysis: Ancient Qin-Han county name ('Hut on the Hill'), later renamed Jizhou in Sui and Ji'an in Yuan.

b_anfu_2.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Anfu County (安福县) in 624 CE (Tang Wude 7) under Jizhou, succeeding Ancheng and Anfu (安复).
b_anfu_2.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Tang-era alteration of Western Jin Anfu (安复) and Qin-Han Ancheng (安成).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Western Han Gaozu 5 (202 BCE) Ancheng; Western Jin Taikang 1 (280 CE) Anfu
older_name_by_867.notes: Succeeded Qin-Han Ancheng and Anping counties, renamed 安复 in 280 CE and 安福 in 624 CE.

b_taihe.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Taihe County (泰和县) in 591 CE (Sui Kaihuang 11), written 太和 in 625 CE (Tang Wude 8).
b_taihe.etymology_analysis: Auspicious name ('Supreme Harmony'), bestowed in 591 CE because 'the land produced auspicious grain born of harmonious qi' (地产嘉禾，和气所生).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Eastern Han Xingping 1 (194 CE) Xichang; Sui Kaihuang 10 (590 CE) Anfeng
older_name_by_867.notes: Founded as Xichang County in 194 CE; briefly Anfeng in 590 CE before becoming Taihe in 591 CE.

b_yongxin.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yongxin County (永新县) in 267 CE (Eastern Wu Baoding 2) under Ancheng Commandery.
b_yongxin.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Eastern Wu county name meaning 'Eternally New'.

b_wanan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Wan'an County (万安县) in 1071 CE (Northern Song Xining 4), split from Longquan and Taihe.
b_wanan.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Northern Song name ('Myriad Peace') bestowed when Wan'an Town was elevated to a county in 1071 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Sui Kaihuang 11 (591 CE) Taihe; Eastern Wu Suixing
older_name_by_867.notes: Part of Taihe County (and earlier Eastern Wu Suixing) prior to Longquan (943 CE) and Wan'an (1071 CE).

b_qingjiang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Qingjiang County (清江县) in 938 CE (Southern Tang Shengyuan 2), seated at Xiaotan Town (萧滩镇).
b_qingjiang.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Qingjiang ('Clear River'), referring to the clear, calm stretch of the Gan/Yuan confluence; renamed Zhangshu in 1988.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Qin Xingan (221 BCE) and Tang Wude 5 (622 CE) Gao'an
older_name_by_867.notes: Split from townships of Gao'an and Xingan in 938 CE.

b_xingan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Xingan County (新淦县) in 221 BCE (Qin dynasty), one of the 18 ancient counties of Yuzhang Commandery.
b_xingan.etymology_analysis: Ancient Qin-Han county name ('New Gan-stream'), located along the Gan River valley; simplified to 新干 in 1957.

b_xinyu.first_mention_attestation: Tang dynasty Tianbao era (742–756 CE) renaming of Xinyu County (新渝县, founded 267 CE under Eastern Wu) to 新喻县 (recorded in Dushi Fangyu Jiyao and Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi).

morphemes.translation: homophonous alteration of Yu River (渝水)

b_xinyu.etymology_analysis: Originally established in 267 CE under Eastern Wu as Xinyu (新渝) after the Yu River (渝水); renamed 新喻 during the Tang Tianbao era (742–756 CE) and simplified to 新余 in 1957 CE.

b_yichun.first_mention_attestation: Western Han dynasty, 6th year of Emperor Gaozu (201 BCE), when Yichun County (宜春县) was established under Yuzhang Commandery.
b_yichun.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Classical Chinese toponym meaning 'fittingly spring-like', traditionally associated with local warm springs and fertile terrain; continuously attested since 201 BCE.

b_fenyi.first_mention_attestation: Northern Song dynasty, 1st year of Yongxi (984 CE), when Fenyi County was carved out of eastern Yichun County under Yuanzhou.
b_fenyi.etymology_analysis: Administrative compound meaning 'divided from Yichun', coined upon its creation as a separate county in 984 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Western Han foundation of Yichun County (201 BCE).
older_name_by_867.notes: Eastern territory of Han-Tang Yichun County before Fenyi was split off in 984 CE.

b_pingxiang.first_mention_attestation: Three Kingdoms Eastern Wu, 2nd year of Baoding (267 CE), when Pingxiang County (萍乡县) was split from Yichun County under Ancheng Commandery.
b_pingxiang.etymology_analysis: Named either after abundant duckweed in local waterways or the legend of King Zhao of Chu finding a 'ping' fruit while crossing the river.

b_gaoan.first_mention_attestation: Tang dynasty, 5th year of Wude (622 CE), when Jiancheng County (建成县) was renamed Gao'an County to avoid the taboo name of Crown Prince Li Jiancheng (recorded in Taiping Huanyu Ji).
b_gaoan.etymology_analysis: Topographic-auspicious name ('high and peaceful') adopted in 622 CE, replacing the earlier Han name Jiancheng (建成, 201 BCE).

b_xinchang.first_mention_attestation: Northern Song dynasty, 6th year of Taiping Xingguo (981 CE), when Xinchang County (新昌县) was established in Yunzhou from former Yifeng territory.
b_xinchang.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Song-era county name ('new and prosperous') created in 981 CE; renamed back to Yifeng (宜丰) in 1914 CE to avoid duplication with Xinchang in Zhejiang.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Three Kingdoms Eastern Wu, Huangwu era (222–229 CE), split from Jiancheng County.
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally founded as Yifeng County under Eastern Wu before being merged into Jiancheng/Gao'an and later revived as Xinchang in 981 CE.

b_shanggao.first_mention_attestation: Southern Tang, 10th year of Baoda (952 CE), when Shanggao Garrison (上高镇, itself established 881–884 CE) was elevated to Shanggao County.
b_shanggao.etymology_analysis: Topographic descriptor ('upper high') referring to elevated terrain along the Jin River; first attested as a garrison in 881–884 CE and as a county in 952 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Western Jin / Eastern Wu records (Jinshu Dili Zhi).
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Wangcai County covered the Shanggao area prior to the late-Tang/Southern Tang establishment of Shanggao.

b_dayu.first_mention_attestation: Sui dynasty, 10th year of Kaihuang (590 CE), when Anyuan Commandery was reorganized as Dayu County (大庾县), restored in 705 CE under Tang Shenlong 1.
b_dayu.etymology_analysis: Named directly after Dayu Ridge (大庾岭), the principal pass of the Nanling Mountains between Jiangxi and Guangdong.

b_shangyou.first_mention_attestation: Southern Tang, 10th year of Baoda (952 CE), when Shangyou Chang (上犹场) was elevated to Shangyou County.

morphemes.translation: You River / Mount Dayou (犹水 / 大犹山)

b_shangyou.etymology_analysis: Locator compound meaning 'above the mouth of the You River (south of Mount Dayou)'; established as a county in 952 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Western Jin Taikang 1 (280 CE) renaming of Nan'an County.
older_name_by_867.notes: Shangyou was carved out of western Nankang County in the Five Dynasties / Southern Tang period.

b_nankang.first_mention_attestation: Western Jin dynasty, 1st year of Taikang (280 CE), when Nan'an County (南安县) was renamed Nankang County (南康县).
b_nankang.etymology_analysis: Directional-auspicious name ('southern peace/prosperity') adopted in 280 CE under Western Jin.

b_yudu.first_mention_attestation: Western Han dynasty, 6th year of Emperor Gaozu (201 BCE), when Yudu County (雩都县) was established.
b_yudu.etymology_analysis: Named after Mount Yu (雩山) to the north of the county seat combined with 都 ('chief settlement'); simplified to 于都 in 1957 CE.

b_huichang.first_mention_attestation: Northern Song dynasty, 7th year of Taiping Xingguo (982 CE), when Huichang County was split from Yudu County.
b_huichang.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Song-era county name ('converging prosperity') created in 982 CE from southeastern Yudu County.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Western Han Gaozu 6 (201 BCE) foundation of Yudu County.
older_name_by_867.notes: Part of Yudu County prior to Huichang's creation in 982 CE.

b_qianhua.first_mention_attestation: Liu Song dynasty, 5th year of Daming (461 CE), when Qianhua County (虔化县) was split from Ningdu County; restored in 598 CE (Sui Kaihuang 18).
b_qianhua.etymology_analysis: Auspicious administrative name ('reverent transformation') first attested in 461 CE and serving as the Tang-era name of modern Ningdu until 1153 CE.

b_ruijin.first_mention_attestation: Southern Tang, 11th year of Baoda (953 CE), when Ruijin Jian (瑞金监, created in 904 CE) was elevated to Ruijin County.
b_ruijin.etymology_analysis: Auspicious name ('auspicious gold') referencing alluvial gold deposits; first attested as Ruijin Jian in 904 CE and as a county in 953 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Eastern Han, 7th year of Jian'an (202 CE), establishment of Xianghu Town under Yudu County.
older_name_by_867.notes: Xianghu Town (象湖镇) was the Han-through-Tang predecessor settlement on the Ruijin site before 904 CE.

b_gan.first_mention_attestation: Western Han dynasty, 6th year of Emperor Gaozu (201 BCE), when Gan County (赣县) was established at the confluence of the Zhang and Gong rivers.
b_gan.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Gan River (赣江), formed at the confluence of the Zhang and Gong rivers; attested since 201 BCE.

b_anyuan.first_mention_attestation: Liang dynasty, 10th year of Datong (544 CE), when Anyuan County (安远县) was split from Yudu County.
b_anyuan.etymology_analysis: Imperial frontier-pacification name ('pacifying the distant') coined in 544 CE.

b_lishui_1.first_mention_attestation: Tang dynasty, 4th year of Wude (621 CE), when Lishui County was briefly established (merged 625 CE; Kuocang County permanently renamed Lishui in 779 CE, Dali 14).
b_lishui_1.etymology_analysis: Descriptive hydronymic compound ('beautiful water') referring to the Oujiang / Haoxi river system; first established as a county in 621 CE and permanently named in 779 CE.

b_longquan_1.first_mention_attestation: Tang dynasty, 2nd year of Qianyuan (759 CE), when Longquan County (龙泉县) was split from Songyang and Suichang counties (Longquan Township 龙泉乡 named in 620 CE).
b_longquan_1.etymology_analysis: Originally Longyuan Township (龙渊乡, 323 CE), renamed Longquan (龙泉) in 620 CE to avoid the taboo name of Emperor Gaozu of Tang (Li Yuan 李渊).

b_songyang.first_mention_attestation: Eastern Han dynasty, 4th year of Jian'an (199 CE), when Songyang County (松阳县) was split from Zhang'an County.
b_songyang.etymology_analysis: Topographic `-yang` compound ('sunny pine slope'), the oldest county in the Lishui basin, continuously attested since 199 CE.

b_qingtian.first_mention_attestation: Tang dynasty, 2nd year of Jingyun (711 CE), when Qingtian County (青田县) was split from Kuocang County (name also attested in Liu Song Yongjia Junji).
b_qingtian.etymology_analysis: Descriptive topographic compound ('azure field') named after Mount Qingtian (青田山) and local dye-grass/fungi traditions.

b_jinyun.first_mention_attestation: Tang dynasty, 4th year of Wude (621 CE), initial establishment of Jinyun County (re-established in 696 CE, Wu Zhou Wansui Dengfeng 1).
b_jinyun.etymology_analysis: Named directly after Mount Jinyun (缙云山, recorded in Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi: '因山为名'), associated with the mythical Yellow Emperor.

b_mao.first_mention_attestation: Qin dynasty, 25th year of King Zheng of Qin (222 BCE), when Mao County (鄮县) was established under Kuaiji Commandery.
b_mao.etymology_analysis: Ancient Qin-era county name in modern Ningbo (Yinzhou), derived from a pre-imperial Yue toponym and trade port.

b_xiangshan.first_mention_attestation: Tang dynasty, 2nd year of Shenlong (706 CE), when Xiangshan County (象山县) was established.
b_xiangshan.etymology_analysis: Descriptive oronymic compound ('Elephant Mountain') referring to the elephant-shaped ridge on the peninsula; county founded in 706 CE.

b_cixi.first_mention_attestation: Tang dynasty, 26th year of Kaiyuan (738 CE; some sources cite 728 CE), when Cixi County (慈溪县) was split from Mao County.
b_cixi.etymology_analysis: Named after the local Cixi stream ('Compassionate Creek'), honoring Eastern Han filial son Dong An (董黯).

b_wengshan.first_mention_attestation: Tang dynasty, 26th year of Kaiyuan (738 CE), when Wengshan County (翁山县) was established on Zhoushan Island.
b_wengshan.etymology_analysis: Descriptive oronymic compound ('Elder Mountain/Island') referring to Zhoushan Island; founded as Wengshan County in 738 CE.

b_linhai.first_mention_attestation: Three Kingdoms Eastern Wu, Huangwu–Huanglong era (222–231 CE), when Linhai County (临海县) was split from Zhang'an and Yongning.
b_linhai.etymology_analysis: Locator compound meaning 'overlooking the sea', attested since the early 3rd century CE.

b_lean.first_mention_attestation: Eastern Jin dynasty, 3rd year of Yonghe (347 CE), when Le'an County (乐安县) was established (later renamed Yong'an and in 1007 CE Xianju).
b_lean.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Classical Chinese name ('joyful peace') established in 347 CE; renamed Xianju (仙居) in 1007 CE.

b_huangyan.first_mention_attestation: Wu Zhou dynasty, 1st year of Tianshou (690 CE), when Yongning County (founded 675 CE) was renamed Huangyan County (黄岩县) after Mount Huangyan.
b_huangyan.etymology_analysis: Descriptive oronymic compound ('Yellow Crag') named after Mount Huangyan; established in 690 CE.

b_ninghai.first_mention_attestation: Western Jin dynasty, 1st year of Taikang (280 CE), when Ninghai County (宁海县) was split from northern Linhai County.
b_ninghai.etymology_analysis: Auspicious coastal compound ('tranquil sea') attested since 280 CE.
