b_yongjia.first_mention_attestation: Sui dynasty, 9th year of Kaihuang (589 CE), when Yongning County (founded 138 CE) was renamed Yongjia County (永嘉县).
b_yongjia.etymology_analysis: Auspicious compound ('eternal excellence') inherited from Yongjia Commandery (323 CE) and applied to the county in 589 CE.

b_yuecheng.first_mention_attestation: Eastern Jin dynasty, 2nd year of Ningkang (374 CE), when Yuecheng County (乐成县) was established (renamed Yueqing 乐清 in 908 CE).
b_yuecheng.etymology_analysis: Classical Chinese toponym ('musical completion / joyful citadel') attested in 374 CE; renamed Yueqing (乐清) in 908 CE under Wuyue.

b_angu.first_mention_attestation: Western Jin dynasty, 1st year of Taikang (280 CE), when Anyang County (Eastern Wu) was renamed Angu County (安固县).
b_angu.etymology_analysis: Auspicious compound ('peaceful and secure') adopted in 280 CE; renamed Rui'an (瑞安) in 902 CE.

b_hengyang.first_mention_attestation: Western Jin dynasty, Taikang era (shortly after 283 CE / Taikang 4), when Shiyang County (始阳县) was renamed Hengyang County (横阳县).
b_hengyang.etymology_analysis: Topographic `-yang` compound named after Hengyu (横屿) and the Hengjiang River (横江); renamed Pingyang (平阳) in 914 CE under Wuyue.

b_jinhua.first_mention_attestation: Sui dynasty, 18th year of Kaihuang (598 CE), when Dongyang County (formerly Changshan / Wuning) was renamed Jinhua County (金华县).
b_jinhua.etymology_analysis: Auspicious-oronymic name ('golden splendor') derived from Mount Jinhua; attested at the county level since 598 CE.

b_puyang_1.first_mention_attestation: Tang dynasty, 13th year of Tianbao (754 CE), when Puyang County (浦阳县) was established under Wuzhou (renamed Pujiang in 910 CE).
b_puyang_1.etymology_analysis: Hydronymic `-yang` compound named after the Puyang River (浦阳江); established in 754 CE on former Feng'an (195 CE) territory.

b_dongyang.first_mention_attestation: Tang dynasty, 4th year of Chuigong (688 CE), when Dongyang County (东阳县) was split from Yiwu (originally Wuning County, 195 CE).
b_dongyang.etymology_analysis: Directional-topographic compound ('eastern sun') adopted in 688 CE, echoing the earlier Dongyang Commandery (266 CE).

b_yongkang.first_mention_attestation: Three Kingdoms Eastern Wu, 8th year of Chiwu (245 CE), when Yongkang County (永康县) was split from Wushang County.
b_yongkang.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Classical Chinese compound ('eternal peace and health') continuously attested since 245 CE.

b_xinan.first_mention_attestation: Western Jin dynasty, 1st year of Taikang (280 CE), when Xin'an County (新安县, founded 192 CE) was renamed Xin'an (信安县).
b_xinan.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Classical Chinese compound ('faithful peace') adopted in 280 CE; later renamed Xi'an (西安) and modern Quzhou.

b_longqiu.first_mention_attestation: Tang dynasty, 8th year of Zhenguan (634 CE), when Taimo County (太末县, Qin) was renamed Longqiu County (龙丘县).
b_longqiu.etymology_analysis: Descriptive oronymic compound ('Dragon Hill') named after Mount Longqiu (龙丘山); renamed Longyou (龙游) in 931 CE under Wuyue.

b_xujiang.first_mention_attestation: Tang dynasty, 4th year of Wude (621 CE), when Xujiang County (须江县) was split from Xin'an County (abolished 625 CE, restored 689 CE).
b_xujiang.etymology_analysis: Named after the Xujiang Stream (须江溪) south of the county seat; renamed Jiangshan (江山) in 931 CE.

b_kuaiji.first_mention_attestation: Qin dynasty, 25th year of King Zheng of Qin (222 BCE), establishment of Kuaiji Commandery (会稽郡); Kuaiji County (会稽县) formed in 589 CE.
b_kuaiji.etymology_analysis: Named directly after Mount Kuaiji (会稽山), where Yu the Great is said to have assembled the lords to reckon merit; attested since 222 BCE.

b_yuyao.first_mention_attestation: Qin dynasty (c. 222–210 BCE), when Yuyao County (余姚县) was established under Kuaiji Commandery.
b_yuyao.etymology_analysis: Ancient toponym traditionally linked to the Yao clan (descendants of Shun) or a Sinicized Baiyue placename, attested since the Qin dynasty.

b_zhuji.first_mention_attestation: Qin dynasty, 25th year of King Zheng of Qin (222 BCE), when Zhuji County (诸暨县) was established under Kuaiji Commandery.
b_zhuji.etymology_analysis: Ancient Sinicized Baiyue toponym (formerly associated with the Yue state), continuously attested as a county since 222 BCE.

b_shan_1.first_mention_attestation: Western Han dynasty, 4th year of Emperor Jing (153 BCE), when Shan County (剡县) was established (place name Shan also attested under Qin).
b_shan_1.etymology_analysis: Ancient Qin-Han toponym of uncertain Baiyue origin (glossed in Classical Chinese as 'sharp'), continuously attested since at least 153 BCE; later renamed Sheng County (嵊县).

b_qiantang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Qiantang County (錢唐縣) under Kuaiji Commandery by the Qin dynasty in 222 BCE; later elevated to Qiantang Commandery in 587 CE.

morphemes.translation: coin / money (originally Qian clan or embankment)

b_qiantang.etymology_analysis: Originally written 錢唐 (Qiantang), referring to an embankment or dyke built along the Qiantang River estuary (traditionally associated with the local Qian clan or seawall); later standardized as 錢塘.

b_yuhang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yuhang County (餘杭縣) under Kuaiji Commandery during the Qin dynasty (222 BCE), and later served as the seat of Hang Prefecture in 589 CE.
b_yuhang.etymology_analysis: Likely a Sinicized transcription of an ancient Baiyue toponym (Old Chinese *la-gang), later folk-etymologized in Chinese sources as 'Yu's Ferry' (禹杭) or 'surplus ferry crossing'.

b_yuqian.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yuqian County (於潛縣) during the Qin dynasty (c. 222 BCE) and continued as a county under Hang Prefecture throughout the Tang dynasty.
b_yuqian.etymology_analysis: Derived from the classical Chinese/Yue place name 於潛 (Yuqian), associated with local mountain streams and caves in western Hangzhou.

b_fuyang_1.first_mention_attestation: Originally founded as Fuchun County (富春縣) in 221 BCE under the Qin dynasty, it was renamed Fuyang County (富陽縣) in 394 CE during the Eastern Jin dynasty due to an imperial naming taboo.

morphemes.translation: sunny south slope / north bank of river

b_fuyang_1.etymology_analysis: Renamed from Fuchun (富春) to Fuyang (富陽) in 394 CE to avoid the taboo character 'chun' (春) in the name of Empress Dowager Zheng Achun, while retaining 'fu' (wealthy) and adding the toponymic suffix -yang.

b_wucheng_2.first_mention_attestation: Established as Wucheng County (烏程縣) by the Qin dynasty in 222 BCE on the site of Chu's Gucheng County (248 BCE).
b_wucheng_2.etymology_analysis: Traditionally derived from the local Wu (烏) and Cheng (程) clans noted for winemaking in antiquity, or from an earlier Yue/Chu settlement name.

b_anji.first_mention_attestation: Established as Anji County (安吉縣) in 185 CE (Zhongping 2nd year of the Eastern Han dynasty) when split from Guzhang County.
b_anji.etymology_analysis: Auspicious imperial county name meaning 'peaceful and auspicious', reportedly inspired by a passage in the Classic of Poetry (Shijing): '安且吉兮' (peaceful and auspicious).

b_wukang.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Wukang County (武康縣) in 280 CE (Taikang 1st year of the Western Jin dynasty), succeeding Yong'an County under Wuxing Commandery.
b_wukang.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Western Jin county name combining 'wu' (martial) and 'kang' (peace/vigor), replacing the earlier Three Kingdoms name Yong'an (永安).

b_jiande.first_mention_attestation: Created as the Marquisate of Jiande (建德侯國) in 221 CE for Sun Shao by Sun Quan of Eastern Wu, and converted into Jiande County (建德縣) in 225 CE.
b_jiande.etymology_analysis: Coined by Sun Quan in 221 CE from the phrase '建功立德' (establishing merit and virtue) when enfeoffing his general Sun Shao.

b_suian.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Sui'an County (遂安縣) in 280 CE (Taikang 1st year of the Western Jin dynasty), succeeding Xinding County (established 208 CE).
b_suian.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Western Jin administrative renaming of Xinding County (新定縣), expressing the wish for complete peace and stability.

b_shouchang_1.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Shouchang County (壽昌縣) in 280 CE (Taikang 1st year of the Western Jin dynasty), succeeding Xinchang County (established 225 CE).
b_shouchang_1.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Western Jin renaming of Eastern Wu's Xinchang County (新昌縣) in 280 CE, signifying longevity and prosperity.

b_qingxi.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Qingxi County (青溪縣 / 清溪縣) in 805 CE (Yongzhen 1st year of the Tang dynasty) from Huanchun County due to the naming taboo of Emperor Xianzong (Li Chun).
b_qingxi.etymology_analysis: Descriptive compound meaning 'clear stream', adopted in 805 CE to replace Huanchun (還淳) after Li Chun ascended the Tang throne.

b_jiaxing.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Jiaxing County (嘉興縣) in 242 CE during the Eastern Wu state of the Three Kingdoms (replacing Hexing/Jiahe due to the naming taboo of Crown Prince Sun He).
b_jiaxing.etymology_analysis: Auspicious county name meaning 'auspicious prosperity', replacing Hexing (禾興) in 242 CE to avoid the character 'he' (禾/和) in Sun He's name.

b_huating.first_mention_attestation: Established as Huating County (華亭縣) in 751 CE (Tianbao 10th year of the Tang dynasty) by Zhao Juzhen, governor of Wu Commandery.
b_huating.etymology_analysis: Named after the Huating Valley / post-station in the Songjiang area, attested since the Three Kingdoms/Jin period and formalized as a Tang county in 751 CE.

b_haiyan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Haiyan County (海鹽縣) under Kuaiji Commandery during the Qin dynasty (222–221 BCE).
b_haiyan.etymology_analysis: Literally 'sea salt', named after the coastal salt-panning industry along Hangzhou Bay in antiquity.

b_anlu.first_mention_attestation: Established as Anlu County (安陸縣) under Nan Commandery following the Qin conquest of Chu in 223 BCE.
b_anlu.etymology_analysis: Named for its relatively elevated, dry terrain ('settled on dry land') above the surrounding Yunmeng marshlands, or associated with the Luhun (陸渾) migrants.

b_yingshan.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Yingshan County (應山縣) in 598 CE (Kaihuang 18th year of the Sui dynasty), succeeding Yongyang County.
b_yingshan.etymology_analysis: Named in 598 CE under the Sui dynasty after the local mountain and Ying Prefecture (應州).

b_yunmeng.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yunmeng County (雲夢縣) in 550 CE (Datong 16th year of the Western Wei) at the ancient Yunmeng city, named after the pre-Qin Yunmeng Marsh (雲夢澤) attested in the Zuo Zhuan and Zhouli.
b_yunmeng.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the ancient Yunmeng Marsh (雲夢澤), a vast wetland complex in Chu where 'meng' (夢) reflects an ancient Chu dialectal word for marshland.

b_xiaochang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Xiaochang County (孝昌縣) in 454 CE during the Liu Song dynasty (Southern Dynasties).
b_xiaochang.etymology_analysis: Named 'filial piety and prosperity' in 454 CE in honor of celebrated local exemplars of filial piety such as Dong Yong, Huang Xiang, and Meng Zong.

b_jiangxia.first_mention_attestation: Established as Jiangxia Commandery (江夏郡) in 201 BCE during the Western Han dynasty, and later as Jiangxia County (江夏縣) in 589 CE under the Sui dynasty.
b_jiangxia.etymology_analysis: Named after the confluence of the Yangtze River (江) and the Xia River (夏水, an ancient distributary/tributary in the Jianghan Plain).

b_puqi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Puqi County (蒲圻縣) in 223 CE (Huangwu 2nd year of Eastern Wu) during the Three Kingdoms period.
b_puqi.etymology_analysis: Named after the reed-lined (蒲) shores and riverbanks (圻) of the local lake/river system when Eastern Wu established the county in 223 CE.

b_wuchang.first_mention_attestation: Named Wuchang (武昌) in 221 CE when Sun Quan of Eastern Wu moved his capital to E County (modern Ezhou) and renamed it.
b_wuchang.etymology_analysis: Coined by Sun Quan in 221 CE from the slogan '以武而昌' ('prospering through martial prowess') when making it Eastern Wu's capital.

b_tangnian.first_mention_attestation: Established as Tangnian County (唐年縣) in 743 CE (Tianbao 2nd year of the Tang dynasty), split from Puqi County under E Prefecture.
b_tangnian.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Tang dynasty county name meaning 'Years of Tang', established in 743 CE and later renamed Chongyang (崇陽) in the 10th century.

b_yongxing_2.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Yongxing County (永興縣) in 589 CE (Kaihuang 9th year of the Sui dynasty), succeeding Fuchuan County.
b_yongxing_2.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Sui dynasty renaming of Fuchuan County (富川縣) in 589 CE, meaning 'eternal prosperity'.

b_huanggang.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Huanggang County (黃岡縣) in 598 CE (Kaihuang 18th year of the Sui dynasty), succeeding Nan'an County under Huang Prefecture.
b_huanggang.etymology_analysis: Named in 598 CE after Mount Huanggang (黃岡山), whose name combines 'huang' (yellow earth or the ancient State of Huang) and 'gang' (ridge).

b_macheng.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Macheng County (麻城縣) in 598 CE (Kaihuang 18th year of the Sui dynasty), succeeding Xin'an County.
b_macheng.etymology_analysis: Named after the ancient Macheng fortification built in the region (traditionally linked to Zhao Shizhen or local hemp cultivation) and adopted as the county name in 598 CE.

b_huangpi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Huangpi County (黃陂縣) in 579 CE (Daxiang 1st year of the Northern Zhou dynasty) near the ancient Huangcheng fortress.
b_huangpi.etymology_analysis: Named in 579 CE after the local reservoir/embankment (陂) and the Huang clan/fortress (黃城) of the region.

b_qichun.first_mention_attestation: Established as Qichun County (蘄春縣) in 201 BCE (6th year of Emperor Gaozu of Western Han) under Jiangxia Commandery.
b_qichun.etymology_analysis: Named after the Qi River (蘄水) and the medicinal/aromatic Qi herb (蘄艾/蘄草) native to the area, combined with the auspicious element 'chun' (spring).

b_huangmei.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Huangmei County (黃梅縣) in 598 CE (Kaihuang 18th year of the Sui dynasty), succeeding Yongxing County under Qi Prefecture.
b_huangmei.etymology_analysis: Named in 598 CE after Mount Huangmei (黃梅山) and the Huangmei River, with 'huang' also linked to the displaced people of the ancient State of Huang.

b_guangji.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Guangji County (廣濟縣) in 742 CE (Tianbao 1st year of the Tang dynasty), succeeding Yongning County under Qichun Commandery.
b_guangji.etymology_analysis: Tang dynasty renaming of Yongning County (永寧縣) in 742 CE, meaning 'broad relief' or 'vast ferry crossing' along the Yangtze.

b_qishui.first_mention_attestation: Established as Qishui County (蘄水縣) in 448 CE (Yuanjia 25th year of the Liu Song dynasty), and restored under that name in 598 CE under the Sui dynasty.
b_qishui.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Qishui River (蘄水, modern Xishui River), a northern tributary of the Yangtze in eastern Hubei.

b_baling.first_mention_attestation: Established as Baling County (巴陵縣) in 280 CE (Taikang 1st year of the Western Jin dynasty), split from Xiajun County.
b_baling.etymology_analysis: Traditionally derived from the legend of Hou Yi slaying a giant Ba serpent at Dongting Lake whose bones formed a mound (陵), or from the hills overlooking Dongting.

b_changjiang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Changjiang County (昌江縣) in 707 CE (Shenlong 3rd year of the Tang dynasty), split from eastern Xiangyin County.
b_changjiang.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the local Changjiang (昌江 / 昌水) river when split from Xiangyin in 707 CE; later renamed Pingjiang (平江) in 923 CE.

b_linxiang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Linxiang County (臨湘縣) in 996 CE (Zhidao 2nd year of the Northern Song dynasty), renamed from Wangchao County (994 CE).
b_linxiang.etymology_analysis: Named in 996 CE for overlooking the confluence of the three Xiang waterways (Sanxiang) and the Yangtze; distinct from the ancient Han-era Linxiang County at Changsha.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Jin (Jin Shu), Western Jin Taikang 1st year (280 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Prior to the Five Dynasties Wangchao Market (934–936 CE) and Northern Song Linxiang County (996 CE), the territory was administered as part of Baling County (established 280 CE).

b_xiangyin.first_mention_attestation: Established as Xiangyin County (湘陰縣) in 474 CE (Yuanhui 2nd year of the Liu Song dynasty) and listed in the Book of Song.
b_xiangyin.etymology_analysis: Named for its location on the southern ('yin', 陰) side of the Xiang River / Dongting outlet.

b_jingling.first_mention_attestation: Established as Jingling County (竟陵縣) during the Qin/early Western Han period (c. 206 BCE) under Jiangxia Commandery.
b_jingling.etymology_analysis: Literally 'the end of the hills', referring to the southern terminus of the Dahong Mountain foothills where they meet the Jianghan Plain.

b_mianyang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Mianyang County (沔陽縣) and Mianyang Commandery in the mid-6th century (c. 551 CE) during the Southern Liang dynasty.
b_mianyang.etymology_analysis: Named for its position on the northern ('yang', 陽) side of the Mian River (an ancient name for the lower Han River).

b_jianli.first_mention_attestation: First established as Jianli County (監利縣) under Eastern Wu during the Three Kingdoms period (c. 222–252 CE), split from Huarong County, and restored under Western Jin in 280 CE.
b_jianli.etymology_analysis: Literally 'supervising revenue', derived from the Eastern Wu official post established to oversee fish and salt taxes (監收魚鹽之利) in the Jianghan wetlands.

b_yusha.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yusha County (玉沙縣) in 965 CE (Qiande 3rd year of the Northern Song dynasty) under Jiangling Prefecture.
b_yusha.etymology_analysis: Named 'jade sand' in the Northern Song period after the bright sandy shoals along the Yangtze and Lake Honghu.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Records of the Three Kingdoms / Book of Jin
older_name_by_867.notes: Before Yusha County was created in 965 CE (Northern Song), the area belonged to Jianli County (established c. 222 CE) and ancient Zhouling County.

b_zigui.first_mention_attestation: Established as Zigui County (秭歸縣) under Nan Commandery in the early Western Han dynasty (c. 202 BCE), on the site of the ancient Chu/Kui state.
b_zigui.etymology_analysis: Traditionally explained as 'elder sister's return' (referring to Qu Yuan's elder sister returning to mourn him, per Shuijingzhu), though linguists also link it to the ancient State of Kui (歸/夔).

b_badong.first_mention_attestation: Established as Badong County (巴東縣) in 598 CE (Kaihuang 18th year of the Sui dynasty), renamed from Lexiang County.
b_badong.etymology_analysis: Literally 'east of Ba', referring to its location at the eastern edge of the ancient Ba region (and earlier Badong Commandery).

b_xingshan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Xingshan County (興山縣) in 260 CE (Yong'an 3rd year of Eastern Wu) under Jianping Commandery, split from northern Zigui County.
b_xingshan.etymology_analysis: Named in 260 CE because the county seat 'rose amidst the mountains' (縣治興建於群山之中).

b_hanyang.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Hanyang County (漢陽縣) in 606 CE (Daye 2nd year of the Sui dynasty), succeeding Hanjin County.
b_hanyang.etymology_analysis: Named in 606 CE for its historic location on the northern ('yang', 陽) bank of the mouth of the Han River where it meets the Yangtze.

b_hanchuan.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Hanchuan County (漢川縣) in 977 CE (Taiping Xingguo 2nd year of the Northern Song dynasty), succeeding Yichuan County due to the naming taboo of Emperor Taizong.
b_hanchuan.etymology_analysis: Named 'Han River' in 977 CE after the Han River flowing through the county, replacing Yichuan (義川) to avoid the taboo character 'yi' (義) in Emperor Taizong's personal name Zhao Guangyi.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Zhou / Old Book of Tang (561 CE Zhenshan; 621 CE Chachuan)
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally founded as Zhenshan County in 561 CE (Northern Zhou) and renamed Chachuan County in 621 CE (Tang Wude 4th year); renamed Yichuan in 960 CE and Hanchuan in 977 CE.

b_jiangling.first_mention_attestation: Established as Jiangling County (江陵縣) under Nan Commandery in 278 BCE after the Qin general Bai Qi captured the Chu capital Ying.
b_jiangling.etymology_analysis: Named for the elevated mounds/ridges (陵) along the northern bank of the Yangtze River (江) protecting the ancient Chu capital Ying from flooding.

b_dangyang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Dangyang County (当阳县) in 148 BCE (2nd year of Zhongyuan, Emperor Jing of Western Han), split from Jiangling County; recorded in the Book of Han (Han Shu, Treatise on Geography).

morphemes.translation: sunny south slope / north bank of river

b_dangyang.etymology_analysis: Chinese 当阳 (Dāngyáng), meaning 'facing the sunny south slope' (or north of the Ju River / south of Mount Jing).

b_jingmen.first_mention_attestation: Established as Jingmen County (荆门县) in 805 CE (21st year of Zhenyuan, Tang dynasty) under Jiangling Prefecture, named as the gateway to Jingzhou.
b_jingmen.etymology_analysis: Chinese 荆门 (Jīngmén), literally 'Gateway to Jingzhou', referring to its strategic pass between the Han River valley and the Jianghan Plain.

b_zhijiang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Zhijiang County (枝江县) in the early Western Han dynasty (c. 202 BCE) under Nan Commandery, named after the branching channels of the Yangtze River; recorded in the Book of Han (Han Shu).
b_zhijiang.etymology_analysis: Chinese 枝江 (Zhījiāng), meaning 'branching river', describing the Yangtze River splitting into multiple channels and islets here.

b_qianjiang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Qianjiang County (潜江县) in 965 CE (3rd year of Qiande, Northern Song dynasty) by elevating Baifu Xunyuan, named after the Qian River distributary of the Han River.
b_qianjiang.etymology_analysis: Chinese 潜江 (Qiánjiāng), from the classical phrase 'Han chu wei Qian' (汉出为潜), referring to a distributary flowing from the Han River toward the Yangtze.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Han Shu, Treatise on Geography)
older_name_by_867.notes: Prior to 965 CE, the area was administered under Jiangling County (江陵县) and Jingling County (竟陵县), both established in the Qin–Han period (c. 202 BCE).

b_wuling.first_mention_attestation: Established as Wuling Commandery (武陵郡) in 202 BCE (5th year of Han Gaozu); later reconstituted as Wuling County (武陵县) in 589 CE (9th year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty) at modern Changde.
b_wuling.etymology_analysis: Chinese 武陵 (Wǔlíng), 'martial hills', derived from the Wuling Commandery and Wuling Mountains of northwestern Hunan.

b_longyang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Longyang County (龙阳县) in 248 CE (11th year of Chiwu, Eastern Wu during the Three Kingdoms period), split from Wushou County (formerly Hanshou).
b_longyang.etymology_analysis: Chinese 龙阳 (Lóngyáng), named after its location on the sunny southern slope of Mount Longyang (龙阳山).

b_taoyuan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Taoyuan County (桃源县) in 963 CE (4th year of Jianlong / 1st year of Qiande, Northern Song dynasty), separated from Wuling County and named after Taohuayuan ('Peach Blossom Spring').
b_taoyuan.etymology_analysis: Chinese 桃源 (Táoyuán), abbreviated from 桃花源 (Taohuayuan, 'Peach Blossom Spring'), the famous literary utopia by Tao Yuanming.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Han Shu); Book of Later Han (Hou Han Shu)
older_name_by_867.notes: Part of Linyuan County (临沅县) in Western Han (202 BCE) and established as Yuannan County (沅南县) in 50 CE before being merged into Wuling County in 589 CE.

b_yuanjiang.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Yuanjiang County (沅江县) in 598 CE (18th year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty), previously Yaoshan County (Liang) and Anle County (589 CE); recorded in the Book of Sui (Sui Shu).
b_yuanjiang.etymology_analysis: Chinese 沅江 (Yuánjiāng), the Yuan River, directly adopting the hydronym of the river whose mouth enters Dongting Lake here.

b_liyang_1.first_mention_attestation: Established as Liyang County (澧阳县) in 283 CE (4th year of Taikang, Western Jin dynasty) under Tianmen Commandery; later made the seat of Lizhou in 589 CE.
b_liyang_1.etymology_analysis: Chinese 澧阳 (Lǐyáng), meaning 'on the sunny (north) bank of the Li River'.

b_cili.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Cili County (慈利县) in 598 CE (18th year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty), formerly Lingyang County, under Chongzhou; recorded in the Book of Sui (Sui Shu).
b_cili.etymology_analysis: Chinese 慈利 (Cílì), an auspicious name meaning 'kind customs and prosperous products' (土俗淳慈，产物得利).

b_anxiang.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Anxiang County (安乡县) in 560 CE (1st year of Tianjia, Chen dynasty) under Yiyang Commandery of Wuzhou, succeeding earlier Zuotang and Nan'an.
b_anxiang.etymology_analysis: Chinese 安乡 (Ānxiāng), 'peaceful township', derived from the earlier Nan'an name or the Marquisate of Anxiang.

b_gongan.first_mention_attestation: Named Gong'an (公安) in 209 CE (14th year of Jian'an, Eastern Han dynasty) when Liu Bei garrisoned at Youjiangkou and renamed his camp Gong'an ('Duke's Peace').
b_gongan.etymology_analysis: Chinese 公安 (Gōng'ān), 'the Duke's Peace', referring to General of the Left (Zuo Gong) Liu Bei stationing there in 209 CE.

b_huarong.first_mention_attestation: Established as Huarong County (华容县) in the Western Han dynasty (c. 202 BCE) in Nan Commandery; the name was later transferred to the modern Hunan site in 598 CE (18th year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty).
b_huarong.etymology_analysis: Chinese 华容 (Huáróng), 'splendid Rong', named after the ancient Spring and Autumn Chu settlement of Rongcheng (容城).

b_yiling.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 278 BCE during the Warring States period when Qin general Bai Qi burned Yiling (夷陵); recorded in the Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji).
b_yiling.etymology_analysis: Chinese 夷陵 (Yílíng), meaning 'level hills' (where the mountains flatten out at the eastern exit of the Three Gorges).

b_yuanan.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Yuan'an County (远安县) in 559 CE (1st year of Wucheng, Northern Zhou dynasty), previously Linju County (140 BCE) and Gao'an County (Eastern Jin).
b_yuanan.etymology_analysis: Chinese 远安 (Yuǎn'ān), 'distant peace', an auspicious frontier name adopted under Northern Zhou.

b_yidu_1.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yidu Commandery (宜都郡) in 210 CE (15th year of Jian'an, Eastern Han dynasty) by Liu Bei, with Zhang Fei as grand administrator; recorded in the Records of the Three Kingdoms (Sanguozhi).
b_yidu_1.etymology_analysis: Chinese 宜都 (Yídū), meaning 'suitable for a capital' (宜于建都).

b_rang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Rang County (穰县) in 272 BCE by the Qin state under Nanyang Commandery; recorded in the Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji) and Book of Han (Han Shu).
b_rang.etymology_analysis: Chinese 穰 (Ráng), referring to lush, abundant grain harvests in the fertile Nanyang Basin.

b_xinye.first_mention_attestation: Established as Xinye County (新野县) in the Western Han dynasty (c. 202 BCE) under Nanyang Commandery; recorded in the Book of Han (Han Shu, Treatise on Geography).
b_xinye.etymology_analysis: Chinese 新野 (Xīnyě), meaning 'new plain', referring to newly drained and cultivated alluvial land in the Nanyang Basin.

b_nanyang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Nanyang Commandery (南阳郡) in 272 BCE (35th year of King Zhaoxiang of Qin) after Qin captured Wan from Chu; recorded in the Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji).
b_nanyang.etymology_analysis: Chinese 南阳 (Nányáng), referring to its position south of Mount Funiu (伏牛山) and north of the Han River.

b_jutan.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Jutan County (菊潭县) in 583 CE (3rd year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty), formerly Li County (郦县), under Dengzhou; recorded in the Book of Sui (Sui Shu).
b_jutan.etymology_analysis: Chinese 菊潭 (Jútán), named after the Jutan ('Chrysanthemum Pool') spring recorded in the Book of Han and Commentary on the Water Classic (Shuijingzhu).

b_neixiang.first_mention_attestation: Named Neixiang County (内乡县) in 956 CE (3rd year of Xiande, Later Zhou dynasty), succeeding the earlier Sui–Tang Jutan County (菊潭县).
b_neixiang.etymology_analysis: Chinese 内乡 (Nèixiāng), 'inner township', contrasting with Zhongxiang (中乡) in the Dan River valley.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Han Shu); Book of Sui (Sui Shu)
older_name_by_867.notes: Established in Qin as Li County (郦县, c. 221 BCE) and renamed Jutan County (菊潭县) in 583 CE under Sui.

b_fangling.first_mention_attestation: Established as Fangling County (房陵县) in the Qin dynasty (c. 221 BCE) under Hanzhong Commandery; recorded in the Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji) and Book of Han (Han Shu).
b_fangling.etymology_analysis: Chinese 房陵 (Fánglíng), 'chambered hills', describing the enclosed mountain basin surrounding the county.

b_zhushan.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Zhushan County (竹山县) during the reign of Emperor Fei of Western Wei (552–554 CE), replacing Ancheng County (安成县); recorded in the Book of Sui (Sui Shu).
b_zhushan.etymology_analysis: Chinese 竹山 (Zhúshān), 'bamboo mountains', named descriptively for the dense bamboo forests covering its surrounding mountains.

b_yongqing.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Yongqing County (永清县) in 562 CE (2nd year of Baoding, Northern Zhou dynasty), formerly Dahong County (大洪县), under Qianzhou and later Tang Fangzhou.
b_yongqing.etymology_analysis: Chinese 永清 (Yǒngqīng), an auspicious administrative name meaning 'eternally pure and tranquil'.

b_shangyong.first_mention_attestation: Established as Shangyong County (上庸县) in the Qin dynasty (c. 221 BCE) under Hanzhong Commandery, on the territory of the ancient State of Yong (庸) conquered by Chu in 611 BCE.
b_shangyong.etymology_analysis: Chinese 上庸 (Shàngyōng), 'Upper Yong', named after the upper reaches of the ancient State of Yong in the Du River valley.

b_wudang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Wudang County (武当县) in 202 BCE (5th year of Han Gaozu) under Hanzhong Commandery, named after the Wudang Mountains; recorded in the Book of Han (Han Shu).
b_wudang.etymology_analysis: Chinese 武当 (Wǔdāng), directly adopting the proper oronym of Mount Wudang (武当山).

b_yunxiang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yunxiang County (郧乡县) in 284 CE (5th year of Taikang, Western Jin dynasty) under Weixing Commandery; later subordinated to Junzhou in Tang.

morphemes.translation: ancient State of Yun / Yun Pass

b_yunxiang.etymology_analysis: Chinese 郧乡 (Yúnxiāng), named after the nearby Yun Pass (郧关) or Mount Yun.

b_fengli.first_mention_attestation: Established as Fengli County (丰利县) in the Northern Zhou dynasty (557–581 CE) under Jia Commandery; transferred to Junzhou in 634 CE (8th year of Zhenguan, Tang dynasty).
b_fengli.etymology_analysis: Chinese 丰利 (Fēnglì), an auspicious administrative name meaning 'abundant benefit'.

b_sui.first_mention_attestation: Attested as the State of Sui (随) in 706 BCE in the Zuo Zhuan; later established as Sui County (随县) and Suizhou (随州, written 隋州 under the Sui dynasty, 581–618 CE).
b_sui.etymology_analysis: Chinese 隋 (Suí), variant of 随 (Suí), the ancient Zhou-era State of Sui in northern Hubei, from which Emperor Wen of Sui took his dynastic title.

b_tangcheng.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Tangcheng County (唐城县) in 596 CE (16th year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty), formerly Xiazha County, under Handong Commandery; restored in 738 CE under Tang.
b_tangcheng.etymology_analysis: Chinese 唐城 (Tángchéng), 'walled city of Tang', named after the Spring and Autumn State of Tang located northwest of Suizhou.

b_zaoyang.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Zaoyang County (枣阳县) in 601 CE (1st year of Renshou, Sui dynasty), replacing Guangchang County to avoid the taboo name of Crown Prince Yang Guang; recorded in the Book of Sui (Sui Shu).
b_zaoyang.etymology_analysis: Chinese 枣阳 (Zǎoyáng), named after Zaoyang Village (枣阳村) in the area when Guangchang County was renamed in 601 CE.

b_guanghua.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Guanghua County (光化县) in 1072 CE (5th year of Xining, Northern Song dynasty) from Qiande County (founded 964 CE), taking its name from Guanghua Jun (named after Tang Zhaozong's Guanghua era, 898–901 CE).
b_guanghua.etymology_analysis: Chinese 光化 (Guānghuà), meaning 'radiant civilizing transformation' (光大王化), derived from the late-Tang Guanghua era name (898–901 CE).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Han (Han Shu, Treatise on Geography)
older_name_by_867.notes: In antiquity the State of Yin (阴国, conquered by Chu in 532 BCE), and in Qin–Han times Zan County (酇县) and Yin County (阴县, c. 221 BCE).

b_biyang_1.first_mention_attestation: Established as Biyang County (比阳县) in the Western Han dynasty (c. 202 BCE) under Nanyang Commandery; later the seat of Tangzhou in the Tang dynasty.
b_biyang_1.etymology_analysis: Chinese 比阳 (Bǐyáng), meaning 'on the sunny (north) bank of the Bi River (比水)'.

b_beiyang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Biyang County (泌阳县) in 742 CE (1st year of Tianbao, Tang dynasty) by renaming Shangma County under Tangzhou (Huai'an Commandery); recorded in the Old and New Books of Tang.
b_beiyang.etymology_analysis: Chinese 泌阳 (Bìyáng), meaning 'on the sunny (north) bank of the Bi River (泌水)'; distinct in character from the older Han-era 比阳 (Bǐyáng) until Ming merged/transferred the name in 1380 CE.

b_fangcheng.first_mention_attestation: Established as Fangcheng County (方城县) under the Northern Wei dynasty (late 5th century CE), replacing earlier Duyang County and named after Mount Fangcheng.
b_fangcheng.etymology_analysis: Chinese 方城 (Fāngchéng), 'square wall/citadel', named after Mount Fangcheng (方城山), a natural mountain barrier used as part of the Chu Great Wall.

b_tongbai.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Tongbai County (桐柏县) in the early Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty (581–583 CE), previously Huai'an County, named after the Tongbai Mountains.
b_tongbai.etymology_analysis: Chinese 桐柏 (Tóngbǎi), directly adopting the proper oronym of the Tongbai Mountains (桐柏山), source of the Huai River.

b_xiangyang.first_mention_attestation: Xiangyang City and County (襄阳县) were established in 201 BCE (6th year of Han Gaozu, Western Han dynasty); recorded in the Book of Han (Han Shu).
b_xiangyang.etymology_analysis: Chinese 襄阳 (Xiāngyáng), meaning 'on the sunny (north) bank of the Xiang River (襄水)'.

b_gucheng.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Gucheng County (谷城县) in 587 CE (7th year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty), replacing Zhuyang County, named after the ancient Spring and Autumn State of Gu (谷国, attested 705 BCE).
b_gucheng.etymology_analysis: Chinese 谷城 (Gǔchéng), 'walled city of Gu', commemorating the ancient Zhou-era State of Gu.

b_lexiang.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 401 CE (5th year of Long'an, Eastern Jin dynasty) when Huan Xuan established Wuning Commandery with its seat at Lexiang County (乐乡县); recorded in the Book of Song (Song Shu).
b_lexiang.etymology_analysis: Chinese 乐乡 (Lèxiāng), 'pleasant township', a historic county seat between Jingmen and Zhongxiang.

b_nanzhang.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Nanzhang County (南漳县) in 598 CE (18th year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty), replacing Si'an County, named after the Zhang River (漳水); recorded in the Book of Sui (Sui Shu).
b_nanzhang.etymology_analysis: Chinese 南漳 (Nánzhāng), a directional hydronymic compound referring to the southern Zhang River (distinct from the northern Zhang River in Hebei/Henan).

b_yicheng.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Yicheng County (宜城县) in 192 BCE (3rd year of Emperor Hui of Western Han), previously Yan County (鄢县); recorded in the Book of Han (Han Shu).
b_yicheng.etymology_analysis: Chinese 宜城 (Yíchéng), 'fitting walled city', replacing the older Warring States name Yan (鄢).

b_changshou.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Changshou County (长寿县) in 551 CE (17th year of Datong, Western Wei dynasty) from Changshou (苌寿县, founded 470 CE under Liu Song), and made the seat of Yingzhou.
b_changshou.etymology_analysis: Chinese 长寿 (Chángshòu), 'longevity', adapted from the earlier Liu Song name 苌寿 (470 CE); renamed Zhongxiang in 1531 CE.

b_fushui.first_mention_attestation: Established as Fushui County (富水县) and Fushui Commandery under Western Wei (c. 554 CE) in Wenzhou; later subordinated to Yingzhou in the Tang dynasty (643 CE).
b_fushui.etymology_analysis: Chinese 富水 (Fùshuǐ), directly adopting the hydronym of the Fushui River northeast of Jingshan.

b_jingshan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Jingshan County (京山县) in 607 CE (3rd year of Daye, Sui dynasty) by merging Jiaoling and Panpo counties, named after Mount Jingyuan (京源山).
b_jingshan.etymology_analysis: Chinese 京山 (Jīngshān), abbreviated from Mount Jingyuan (京源山), the nearby mountain east of the county seat.
